bodyOriginal.text: Promotion: subtly reflective silver-grey glass and tactile physical controls characterise Fisher & Paykel 's Contemporary Style kitchen appliances , designed with versatility for the social heart of the home. The Contemporary appliances are one of three product design styles in the New Zealand company's luxury range, alongside the Minimal and Professional offerings.
Fisher & Paykel explained that each of its curated styles supports architects, designers and homeowners in creating bespoke kitchens with a cohesive aesthetic.
"The advantage is a consistent design language across the appliance collection, from cooking and cooling to wine care and dishwashing," said the brand.

bodyOriginal.alt: Image of the Fisher & Paykel Contemporary ovens

bodyOriginal.text: The Contemporary appliance line is made with brushed silver glass Fisher & Paykel 's Contemporary Style includes flush-fitting ovens and cooktops as well as an expansive ecosystem of complementary appliances, all with the same focus on clean lines, softly silver surfaces and comfortable interaction.
Its aesthetic contrasts with the Minimal Style, where dark colours and dial- and handle-free designs allow the products to recede into the background.

Together, the style families are intended to enable the creation of bespoke spaces befitting the evolving role of the domestic kitchen. Fisher & Paykel explained that once hidden from view, kitchens are now one of the main social spaces in the home.
They attract a constant thrum of activity as families join in meal preparation, guests hover and chat, and daily rituals are tended to.

bodyOriginal.alt: Image of a kitchen in golden wood with marble countertops and walls and Fisher & Paykel contemporary silver-coloured appliances integrated into the cabinetry and island

bodyOriginal.text: The style includes a wide ecosystem of appliances, including ovens and hobs Within this context, the brand's style families bring the "beauty of choice" to architects, designers and homeowners in the luxury market, letting them pick products for both their function and cohesion with a material palette.

For the Contemporary range, Fisher & Paykel focused on a timeless appearance, with clean lines and tonal contrasts. Knowledge of interaction and how people experience the space was also taken into consideration.

The brushed silver glass on the ovens has an "active relationship with its surroundings", said the company, picking up on the tones of surrounding materials like stone and timber and gently shifting its appearance as the light changes throughout the day.

bodyOriginal.alt: Close-up image of a Fisher & Paykel contemporary oven showing a soft, subtly reflective coloured finish with a precisely machined knob next to a touchscreen

bodyOriginal.text: The silver-grey glass is subtly reflective "The silver-grey glass finish was designed to create depth and subtle reflectivity within the kitchen," said Fisher & Paykel head of industrial design (cooking) Adam Moody.
"As light changes throughout the day, the products reveal different qualities and relationships with surrounding materials."

The Contemporary range is intended to complement both light and dark interiors, either adding contrast and depth through reflectivity in darker spaces, or reading softly against pale cabinetry, tile and stone.

"With Contemporary Style, we wanted to create a refined material presence: expressive enough to add depth and character to the kitchen, but restrained enough to work across a wide range of architectural interiors," added Moody.

bodyOriginal.alt: Image of a large kitchen with golden wood cabinetry and four Fisher & Paykel ovens installed in a row

This is complemented with intuitive touchscreens and SmartHQ app connectivity for detailed and remote control.
The Contemporary line includes steam, convection and combination ovens as well as companion products such as vacuum seal drawers and warming drawers.

articles.titleOriginal: Clearing Damaged Mitochondria to Fight Skin Photoaging
articles.summaryOriginal: Researchers publishing in Aging Cell have found that a cocktail of molecules released by human umbilical cord mesenchymal stem cells […]

bodyOriginal.text: Researchers publishing in Aging Cell have found that a cocktail of molecules released by human umbilical cord mesenchymal stem cells (hUC-MSCs) can mitigate sun-induced skin aging (photoaging) in mice by restoring their cells’ ability to get rid of their own damaged mitochondria (mitophagy).

Wrinkles are only a small part of the problem Chronic exposure to ultraviolet light is the main driver of photoaging, which is characterized by the accumulation of senescent cells in the skin along with the depletion of DNA-protecting lamins [1]. It causes skin to become thickened, wrinkled, and rough while accumulating visible veins [2]. This damage is more than cosmetic; photoaging can lead to precancerous lesions along with cancer itself [3]. Retinoids and other antioxidants have been found to have some effects but cannot completely reverse this damage [4], and laser-based treatments may be expensive and painful while causing other symptoms [5].

This work focuses on the relationship between the accumulation of damaged mitochondria ( mitochondrial dysfunction ) and age-related inflammation in the absence of pathogens ( inflammaging ). Mitochondrial dysfunction leads to the activation of the inflammatory cGAS-STING pathway [6], which increases the production of cytokines such as IL-6 and IL-8 and is known to drive inflammaging in other tissues [7].

The compounds secreted by hUC-MSCs, including proteins and exosomes, are collectively referred to as the secretome, which has been found to treat diabetic skin lesions in a mouse model [8]. Previous work had involved some of these components, and we have reported extensively on the use of exosomes . However, this team utilized the secretome as a whole, attempting to determine the extent of its effects against mitochondrial dysfunction and inflammaging in the context of skin photoaging.

Broad and significant effects The researchers initially ran a mouse experiment in which they shaved patches of skin and exposed the animals to 40 days of UVA and UVB light calibrated to mimic chronic sun exposure, then treated some of the irradiated skin with a topical hUC-MSC-derived secretome. Compared to the control group, the treated mice showed less epidermal thickening, better hydration, improved elasticity, and less water loss through the skin barrier. Skin collagen, which typically fragments and depletes with ultraviolet exposure, was largely preserved as well. Two markers of cellular senescence, p16 and p21, were also reduced in these animals.

The team also irradiated human skin cells (HaCaT keratinocytes) with UVB and cultured some of them in the presence of an MSC-derived secretome. The results were similar to those seen in mice: compared to the control group, the treated cells were less likely to become senescent as measured by the well-known biomarker SA-β-gal, and they had less UV-induced reduction of Lamin B1.

As expected, compared to mice that were never exposed to ultraviolet radiation at all, exposed mice had more dysfunctional mitochondria and a significant reduction in mitophagy; this was evidenced by increases in mitochondrial proteins, a decrease in the mitophagy biomarker LC3B-II, and similar decreases in the related factors PINK1 and Parkin. These researchers found that treatment with the MSC secretome mitigated this dysfunction completely, as markers of functional mitophagy were indistinguishable from those of the UV-unexposed control group, and these findings were also replicated in vitro with HaCaT cells. Similarly, treatment with this secretome reduced activation of cGAS/STING and diminished the production of downstream inflammatory cytokines, both in mouse skin and in cultured cells.

A clear causal chain Mitophagy was confirmed to be the key driver of the hUC-MSC secretome’s effects. Alongside administration of Mdivi-1, which blocks mitophagy, this secretome was found to be ineffective. Directly blocking STING through the H151 inhibitor, or forcing mitophagy through the compound CCCP, had similar effects as secretome administration in vitro . A series of in vivo experiments utilizing combinations of these compounds confirmed this hierarchical relationship: the hUC-MSC secretome induces mitophagy, which fights cGAS/STING-related inflammation, which is responsible for many of the downstream negative effects of photoaging.

Of course, these experiments were conducted with mice and a single immortalized human skin cell line; as human skin is thicker than mouse skin and has likely suffered different long-term damage over a longer lifespan, the results of a clinical trial may be different. These researchers also chose to use the MSC secretome as a whole rather than specific proteins or exosomes, which obfuscates the contributions of its various components.

However, this study confirms that the skin, just like the heart and brain, experiences inflammaging driven by mitochondrial dysfunction. If the particular factors involved in the hUC-MSC secretome’s effects against this dysfunction can be identified, clinically tested, and produced, such a product may be more effective than current treatment methods.

bodyOriginal.text: AI model that reads heart scans becomes the first of its kind authorized by the FDA to catch heart attacks that standard readings can miss.

Every 40 seconds, someone in the US has a heart attack. The tool doctors reach for first is the electrocardiogram (ECG), which has been around for more than a century and is still the fastest way to check what’s going on inside a patient’s heart. There’s a catch that doesn’t come up enough outside cardiology circles, though: standard interpretation of that test misses a meaningful chunk of acute heart attacks, particularly a category called STEMI equivalents, patterns that mean an artery is blocked without showing the textbook signs doctors are trained to catch right away. Missed reads mean delayed treatment, and in a condition where minutes decide how much heart muscle survives, that delay is often the whole ballgame.

Powerful Medical , based in New York, announced on 4 September that the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) granted its AI-powered ECG model, called Queen of Hearts , De Novo authorization, the agency’s pathway for devices genuinely novel enough that they don’t fit an existing category. First FDA authorization ever given to an AI ECG tool built specifically to catch acute heart attacks, including the equivalents that are easy to miss [ 1 ].

It’s not replacing a cardiologist. Queen of Hearts runs inside a platform called PMcardio, which threads AI-assisted ECG interpretation through the earliest points of contact a patient has with the health system: a paramedic in an ambulance, an ER nurse, the first physician on the chart and hands that assessment off to cardiology faster than a manual read usually allows.

The system reads standard 12-lead ECGs and flags patterns consistent with a heart attack in progress, aiming to close the gap between when a patient’s heart starts struggling and when a cardiologist actually finds out.

More than 20 peer-reviewed studies back the model, according to the company, including randomized controlled trials in major cardiovascular journals, covering upwards of 40,000 patients across four continents. That published data has Queen of Hearts catching roughly twice as many true heart attacks as standard-of-care interpretation, cutting false positives by as much as fivefold, and getting patients to treatment quicker.

It’s already got a track record in Europe. Following CE-marking there, Powerful Medical says the tool detected more than 120,000 heart attacks in 2025, and in over half those cases, helped speed up treatment.
Martin Herman, the company’s CEO and co-founder, treated the FDA decision as much an access story as a technical one.

“This milestone reflects our mission to ensure every patient has access to fast, accurate heart attack diagnosis, regardless of where they present,” he said. “With FDA De Novo authorization in place, we can scale adoption and bring this technology into routine clinical care across the United States.”
(L–R:) Martin Herman (CEO), Robert Herman (CMO) and Felix Bauer (COO)
Robert Herman, the company’s Chief Medical Officer and co-founder, was blunter about what’s actually at stake for patients.
“Many heart attack patients in the United States still miss the window for life-saving treatment due to delays in diagnosis and inefficient triage,” he said.

Felix Bauer, the company’s COO and co-founder, added, “With FDA-approved technology now available, we can bridge this gap by bringing accurate, real-time ECG interpretation to the first medical contact.”
Where this fits into the longevity conversation

Cardiac AI tools get filed under acute care pretty reflexively, and it’s easy to see why, but heart disease sits at the center of just about every serious conversation about healthy lifespan. It’s still the leading cause of death worldwide, and unlike most chronic conditions tied to aging, a heart attack can end a life or permanently damage heart function, over the course of an afternoon.

The window between when damage starts and when treatment begins is one of the few places in cardiovascular medicine where a single technology shift can meaningfully change outcomes, mostly by protecting the heart muscle that would otherwise be lost in the hours right after an event starts, rather than by preventing the disease years ahead of time.

PMcardio is already used more than 2 million times a year by over 100,000 clinicians, per the company, linking emergency responders, ER staff and cardiologists into one coordination platform. Queen of Hearts also holds Breakthrough Device Designation and sits in the FDA’s Total Product Life Cycle Advisory Program, and Powerful Medical is treating this authorization less as an endpoint and more as the starting gun for a broader US rollout.

bodyOriginal.text: $71 million facility in Vilnius will manufacture patient-by-patient treatments, with ambitions stretching into longevity medicine.

There was a ribbon, a crowd, the usual photo line-up of executives and officials. However, the more interesting detail from the opening in Vilnius is what happens inside the building once the cameras leave: some production runs in there will exist for exactly one person, start to finish.

That’s just how cell and gene therapy works. A patient’s own cells can become the raw material for their own treatment, which sounds almost too neat until you consider what it means for manufacturing. You can’t mass-produce a batch of “someone else.” Northway Biotech built its newest and largest facility around that constraint rather than around it [ 1 ].

Northway Biotech, part of the wider Northway Group, opened what it’s calling the first dedicated cell therapy and personalized medicine center of its kind in the Baltic states. The 3,500-square-meter site sits inside the company’s BIO CITY III development and brings up to 20 independent cGMP-compliant manufacturing lines online – the tightly controlled, clean production environments required before any cell-based therapy can go anywhere near a patient. First customer contracts are already signed.

The timing lines up with an anniversary. It’s been 15 years since Professor Vladas Algirdas Bumelis founded the company operating the site, known locally as Kamieninių ląstelių tyrimų centras, the Stem Cell Research Center.

“Fifteen years ago, we did not have a €61 million ($71 million) center – we had people and ambition. Over the years, we have built practical experience, grown our team, and advanced our cell technology capabilities,” Bumelis said. “Today, we are systematically taking all of this to an entirely new scale. What seemed like the future of medicine 15 years ago is now being created here in Lithuania.”
President Gitanas Nausėda showed up for the opening too, and framed it in terms bigger than one company.

“This center is about people. About scientists who will be able to stay in Lithuania and work with technologies that are shaping the future of medicine. About patients for whom personalized medicine is not an abstract concept, but a real treatment option. And about all of us as a country, proving that we can be not only observers, but creators at the global frontier of science,” he said.
Bumelis put the manufacturing shift in plain terms during remarks at the opening.

“We are accustomed to traditional pharmaceutical manufacturing, where a single process produces medicines for large numbers of patients. Here, in some cases, an entire manufacturing process may be dedicated to just one person. It is a completely different pharmaceutical model – and this is precisely the kind of medicine this center was built for,” Bumelis said.

The site’s early focus includes technologies that reprogram a patient’s own immune cells to hunt down specific cancer cells, plus 3D human tissue models researchers use to test drugs and study regenerative medicine without needing a living patient at every step. It’s slower and more expensive than conventional drug-making. It’s also, arguably, the only realistic path for therapies this personalized.
The longevity angle nobody’s shouting about

Northway doesn’t lead with the longevity pitch, but it’s there if you read past the cancer headlines. The company says its cell biology and tissue engineering work will extend into regenerative medicine more broadly, including research into how tissue ages and whether that process can be slowed or partly reversed. That’s a different mission than treating one disease, and it puts Northway alongside a small but growing group of manufacturers treating cell and tissue technology as infrastructure for aging research generally.

It’s worth remembering that even a great regenerative therapy is only as useful as a company’s ability to actually make it, reliably, safely and at a cost health systems can stomach. That unglamorous manufacturing layer tends to get skipped over in coverage of breakthrough science, but it’s the thing that decides whether a promising lab result ever becomes a treatment someone can actually receive.

The project also feeds a national goal: Lithuania wants life sciences to reach 5% of its GDP by 2030. It was financed through private funds and a loan from the country’s development bank, and Edvinas Grikšas, the Minister of the Economy and Innovation, called it proof that “Lithuania is not only a user of advanced technologies, but also a country where they are created and developed.”
The new center is expected to employ around 100 life sciences professionals, on top of the 200-plus Northway already has across Lithuania, the UK and the US.

bodyOriginal.text: The company has launched The Elysium Longevity Institute, a physician-led clinical program meant to bring rigor to a field full of hype.

Walk into most longevity clinics, and you’ll find a familiar formula: a long menu of supplements, a handful of peptides, maybe an IV drip, and a sales pitch dressed up as science. Elysium Health is trying, deliberately, to be the opposite of that. The New York-based company opened The Elysium Longevity Institute (TELI), which it’s calling the biggest milestone in its history since launching back in 2015 [ 1 ].

The pitch is less about offering the newest intervention and more about deciding, carefully, which interventions actually deserve a patient’s trust. TELI is a personalized, physician-led program built around ongoing clinical oversight rather than a one-time consultation and a shopping list.

The Institute is led by Chief Medical Officer Dr Omar Baker, who spent nearly 15 years in clinical care and healthcare leadership, most recently as Executive Vice President and Deputy Chief Medical Officer at UnitedHealth Group, the country’s largest health care company. He’s working alongside Elysium co-founder and Chief Scientist Dr Leonard Guarente, a Novartis Professor of Biology at Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) whose research helped shape the modern understanding of cellular aging in the first place.

“Longevity medicine has reached an inflection point; scientific advances are arriving faster than ever before,” Baker said. “These advances raise the standard for how they should be delivered. Responsible longevity medicine isn’t defined by access to a particular therapy. It’s defined by thoughtful clinical judgment, individualized care, and rigorous quality standards.”
(L–R): Dr Omar Baker, Dr Leonard Guarente and Eric Marcotulli

Baker explained that individuals seek to understand which health interventions suit them, how those measures function in unison, and how their care ought to adapt as their health progresses. He emphasized that combining these core principles with a commitment to producing new clinical evidence forms a model capable of advancing both individual patient outcomes and the broader medical field. Baker noted that this philosophy drives The Elysium Longevity Institute, expressing his belief that it represents the future of longevity medicine and sets the standard every patient deserves.

In practice, that means patients start with a comprehensive medical intake, after which licensed providers build a protocol around their actual medical history, lifestyle and goals, not a template applied to everyone who walks through the door. At launch, TELI offers 18 longevity-focused protocols spanning prescription medications, peptides, supplements and vitamins, delivered orally, intranasally or by injection, with clinical support built in to adjust the plan as a patient’s health changes over time.

Guarente has spent decades studying why organisms age at the molecular level, work that’s arguably more foundational than commercial, and he frames the Institute as the next logical step from lab bench to exam room.

“For decades, the goal of aging research was to understand why we age,” he said. “Today, we’re entering a new era where many of those discoveries are beginning to translate into interventions that may actually help people live healthier, longer lives. The next challenge is ensuring those discoveries are translated responsibly into clinical practice while continuing to generate the evidence that moves the field forward. The Elysium Longevity Institute represents an important step toward making that vision a reality.”
Elysium co-founder and CEO Eric Marcotulli has been making a version of this argument since the company’s earliest supplement products.

“When we launched Elysium in 2015, our mission was to bring the world’s best aging research out of the lab and into people’s lives,” he said. “Over the past decade, we’ve helped define new categories in longevity, supported more than 20 clinical trials, and demonstrated that scientific rigor and commercial innovation can go hand in hand. Our responsibility isn’t simply to make the latest advances in longevity science available; it’s to evaluate them rigorously, deliver them responsibly, and continue contributing to the evidence that shapes the future of longevity medicine. That’s the standard we’ve worked to uphold for more than a decade, and it’s the standard that will define the Institute.”

The longevity supplement market has exploded over the past several years, but so has consumer skepticism, fueled by a steady stream of products that promise more than the underlying research can support. Elysium’s bet is that what serious longevity consumers actually want isn’t a bigger menu of interventions’ it’s someone qualified telling them which ones are worth their time, money and, frankly, their trust.

TELI is currently open to eligible patients in the United States through elysiumhealthrx.com, and Elysium says its protocol list will keep expanding as new therapies clear the same evidentiary bar the company says it’s held itself to since 2015. Whether that bar holds up under real clinical scrutiny is something only time and outcomes data will tell. But as a statement of intent, in a field where “physician-led” too often just means a doctor’s name on a website, launching an actual clinical institute is a meaningfully different kind of bet.

bodyOriginal.text: Inside the assumptions and interactive model behind our $617b longevity biotech TAM – and why you need not agree with us.
With thanks to MuseCell Innovations , sponsor of the Longevity Biotech Report.

Put $617 billion on a market forecast and it has a habit of becoming the story. However, in our new Longevity Biotech Report , which was released yesterday , the more interesting question is not the size of the number but how we arrived at it – and what happens when the assumptions beneath it change.

Our $617b estimate is a target addressable market (TAM): a top-down model of the annual global revenue a future gerotherapeutics market could generate by 2045. It is conditional, not a valuation of the longevity companies and therapeutics that exist today. That distinction matters. The model asks what might happen if approved interventions targeting the biology of aging become available, and builds an answer from assumptions about eligibility, pricing, adoption and timing.

Longevity.Technology: A TAM calculation can acquire the authority of fact remarkably quickly once a sufficiently large dollar sign is placed in front of it. We would rather show our working. The $617 billion figure is an argument about what a future gerotherapeutics market could look like, not a prophecy about what it inevitably will; underneath it sit assumptions about who receives these therapies, when they receive them, what they cost, how quickly they are adopted and when the regulatory starting gun is fired. We have our answers to those questions, but the more interesting exercise is not insisting that everyone shares them.

The TAM Explorer puts those assumptions into the reader’s hands: dial down uptake, push approval further out, change the eligible population or choose another pricing model and $617 billion duly disappears, replaced by your number. Forecasting a market that does not yet exist inevitably involves uncertainty; making that uncertainty adjustable turns a headline prediction into something people can test.

The default model begins with a global market, but does not simply multiply the world’s eligible population by US drug prices. It incorporates regional price erosion to reflect the substantial differences in pharmaceutical pricing between the US and other markets.

Eligibility begins at 45 – a deliberately preventive scenario in which gerotherapeutics are administered before significant age-related morbidity, rather than reserved for older patients who already have disease. The Explorer also allows later starting ages, including over-60 and over-75 populations.

For price, we use GLP-1 therapies as the closest current analogue for a scalable intervention, at approximately $6,000 per patient per year. Alternatives range from cheaper, statin-like economics to considerably more expensive one-time cell and gene therapies.

Then comes uptake. Our default is 35% of the eligible population, reached over a ten-year diffusion curve; the report compares that assumption with adoption of mass-market preventives such as statins and newer GLP-1 therapies. Finally, the clock begins with the first approved gerotherapeutic in 2035 – another assumption examined separately in the report rather than treated as a certainty.
Change any of these and the market changes with it. That is rather the point.
The $617b figure should not be confused with another headline number in the report: $230b.

That estimate comes from the opposite direction. Using our DLT intelligence platform , we individually valued 3,036 therapeutic assets across 781 tracked companies, applying clinical-stage probability and comparable-drug sales data to estimate potential annual revenue through existing disease approval pathways. The methodology includes finite-market caps and removes duplicate molecule entries to guard against inflating the aggregate value.

So $617b is top-down and conditional; $230b is bottom-up and asset-based. One describes the potential market if a new gerotherapeutic category emerges, while the other asks what the pipeline we can see today could generate within regulatory pathways that already exist. They are deliberately separate calculations.
Market forecasts are often presented as finished objects, their assumptions tucked somewhere considerably less prominent than their conclusions. We wanted ours to remain open.

The Longevity Biotech TAM Explorer therefore allows users to alter the variables themselves – testing different populations, prices, uptake rates and timelines, whether their view of the emerging market is more cautious than ours or considerably more ambitious.
Phil Newman is the founder and CEO of Longevity.Technology and an author on our brand-new Longevity Biotech Report

“The $617b figure is our view of where this market could go, based on assumptions we’re happy to put in plain sight,” says Phil Newman, founder and CEO of Longevity.Technology and also an author on the new report . “Rather than asking people to take our word for it, we’ve opened up the model – play with the variables, challenge our thinking and build your own view of what the longevity biotech market could be worth.”
The $617b is our baseline. It need not be yours.

No model can remove the uncertainty inherent in forecasting a therapeutic category almost two decades into the future. It can, however, make that uncertainty visible – and give other people the means to interrogate it.
Perhaps the useful number, then, is not simply $617b. It is whatever the evidence, assumptions and a little judicious slider-moving persuade you the market could become.

bodyOriginal.text: Canadian studio RHAD Architects has completed Two Bay House in Nova Scotia, Canada, which consists of blocky volumes with carved-out voids, mass-timber framing and blackened wood cladding.
The waterfront home is located within a family estate on Cape Breton Island, in northeastern Nova Scotia .

The design began with two simple masses, which were then strategically carved away to form courtyards , terraces and double-height spaces. These voids were designed to "mediate between shelter and landscape".

bodyOriginal.alt: RHAD House view from lake in Nova Scotia

bodyOriginal.text: RHAD Architects has completed Two Bay house in Nova Scotia "The architecture emerges not through the addition of elements, but through a series of deliberate acts of subtraction and carving," said RHAD Architects , a studio based in Dartmouth, Nova Scotia, and led by founder Rayleen Hill.
"The resulting voids are as significant as the forms themselves, becoming the spaces through which the house is experienced."

bodyOriginal.alt: RHAD Architects Two Bay House

bodyOriginal.text: The house is oriented towards a lake The house rises two levels and is partly made of mass timber. Its primary roof structure consists of glue-laminated timber, while the roof decking is standard lumber.
The walls are made of insulated concrete forms (ICFs).

bodyOriginal.alt: Black house with two window bays

bodyOriginal.text: The project is named after its two parallel volumes In plan, it consists of two parallel bars, or "bays", with one shorter in length.
"Their differing lengths establish a protected, west-facing courtyard that shelters outdoor living from prevailing waterfront winds while capturing afternoon sunlight," the team said.

bodyOriginal.alt: Aerial of RHAD Architects Two Bay house

bodyOriginal.text: One "bay" was made shorter to form protected courtyards Exterior walls are clad in vertical wooden siding that was charred using shou sugi ban (yakisugi), an ancient Japanese technique. Treated with black oil, the burnt wood "gives the building a quiet, monolithic presence within the landscape".
In carved-away areas, the solid charred wood gives way to slatted wood and vertical-grain hemlock siding.

bodyOriginal.alt: RHAD Architects Two Bay house close up exterior

bodyOriginal.text: Most of the house was clad with charred wood "The contrast between charred and natural wood makes each subtraction legible, revealing the spaces where the architecture opens itself to light, landscape and occupation," the team said.
The home is entered on the east, where one finds an entry court enclosed within tall, slatted walls.
Filtered sunlight passes into the threshold, creating changing patterns throughout the day, while the enclosure glows in the evening from internal light.

bodyOriginal.alt: RHAD Architects Two Bay house living room interior

bodyOriginal.text: The longer of the two volumes features the living room The vertical space acts as a "constant point of reference" within the home, the team said.
Inside, there is a division between communal and private areas.
The shorter of the two volumes contains two bedrooms on the bottom level and a primary bedroom up above.
The longer volume holds a kitchen, dining area and living room on the ground floor. Upstairs, there is a music room and a small salon, as one of the clients is a hairstylist.

bodyOriginal.alt: RHAD Architects Two Bay house kitchen

bodyOriginal.text: Interior voids and skylights work to bring light into the interior A large portion of the upper floor is carved away, forming a void in the centre of the house. A loft and glass-walled bridge overlook the communal area, "allowing light, conversation and activity to move freely between levels".

Along the water-facing side of the house, ample glazing and covered terraces extend the interior living spaces outward – "allowing the architecture to project into the landscape while maintaining a strong sense of enclosure", the team said.

bodyOriginal.alt: RHAD ARchitects upper floor

bodyOriginal.text: It was designed to show "how subtraction can generate richness" The west side of the house features a swimming pool surrounded by a generous terrace.
Overall, it was designed to show "how subtraction can generate richness," the studio said.
"Rather than relying on formal complexity, it demonstrates how carefully carved voids can produce moments of compression and release, darkness and light, intimacy and openness.
"The result is a home whose character is defined as much by the spaces removed as by those that remain."

bodyOriginal.text: Italy’s South Tyrol province, which borders Switzerland and Austria in the Alps and is home to some of Central Europe’s most dramatic mountains, lives up to its geographic position as a borderland. Italy annexed the region in 1919 following World War I, prior to which it was part of the Austro-Hungarian Empire. Many people are German-speaking, and in many ways, their cultural traditions and ancestry lean traditionally toward Austria more than Italy.

At the outbreak of World War II, the Fascist Italian regime built a series of fortifications along the country’s northernmost border. Construction was halted at the onset of the war, and the military controlled what had been completed until 1993. For Vincenzo Pagliuca , these purpose-built structures spurred an intrepid yet pensive body of work called Bunker, published in hardcover by Hartmann Books.

bodyOriginal.alt: a photograph by Vincenzo Pagliuca of a WWII bunker in South Tyrol

bodyOriginal.text: Many of the bunkers are freestanding concrete masses with distinctive domed shapes and thick walls. Others take advantage of the ancient pre-existing stone, sometimes carving directly into mountainsides and augmenting with extra barriers. Over the years, grasses have colonized the roofs, shrubs have grown close, and some of the exteriors, which were designed to camouflage against the slopes like exposed rock, have a surreal, almost Gaudí-esque character.

Pagliuca has long been fascinated by Italian architecture, such as in his project Mónos , which highlights the often quirky vernacular of diminutive homes. For Bunker, he was interested in the relationship of these specific structures to their rarefied and remote locations, their solidity and often hulking presence at odds with the surrounding Alpine meadows and soaring, snow-capped peaks.

These human interventions, depicted without the presence of people, are a permanent reminder of the drastic measures that political and military forces will go in the name of nationalism. “The bunkers represent a difficult legacy, recalling a dramatic historical period in Central Europe marked by nationalist ideology and the inability to resolve conflicts through peaceful means—an era we thought had long since passed,” says a statement from the publisher.

bodyOriginal.text: AliveCor has launched KardiaACCESS, a 10-year initiative under the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services ACCESS Model, designed to provide clinician-guided, outcome-aligned care focused on blood pressure, blood sugar, and broader cardio-kidney-metabolic health.

The program, the company claims, is available to eligible Original Medicare Part B beneficiaries with no out-of-pocket cost and supplies connected devices, lifestyle coaching, virtual visits, and Kardia app membership.
KardiaACCESS is offered through Kardia Medical Group and is currently available in 48 states, with expansion to Arkansas and South Carolina planned.

The program includes two tracks: an early support track for hypertension, high cholesterol, prediabetes or overweight, and an established condition management track for Type 2 diabetes, chronic kidney disease or existing cardiovascular disease.

The American Heart Association estimates more than 70 percent of U.S. adults aged 60 to 79 live with cardiovascular disease, and CDC data indicate three in four U.S. adults have at least one chronic condition.
The company claims its technology has supported more than 6.4 million patients and recorded over 400 million ECGs.

Rounding out the collection is the Diamond in a Rhinestone World Dolly Doll. Limited to just 1,200 pieces, this doll features an elaborate rhinestone-crusted white suit inspired by one of the many looks fans can see throughout the museum. bodyOriginal.text: American Girl announces Daisy Davenport as its 2027 Girl of the Year , introducing a new character and collection as the brand celebrates its 40th anniversary . From Madison, Wisconsin, Daisy is the first American Girl character from the state and heads to Camp Gowonagin, the same summer camp attended by Historical Character Molly McIntire.

Daisy’s summer takes an unexpected turn when her best friend is unable to attend camp. As she navigates homesickness, new friendships, a fear of the dark, and challenges with her cabin-mates, Daisy learns to step outside her comfort zone and discovers that being a great teammate is about more than being the star player.

“Daisy’s story reflects the enduring spirit of American Girl while bringing a fresh perspective that feels relevant to girls today,” shares Pamela Velarde, Vice President and Head of American Girl. “Her story is a wonderful way to celebrate where American Girl has been and the next chapter.”

The 2027 Girl of the Year collection includes an 18-inch Daisy Davenport doll with green eyes and long auburn-red hair with bangs. The doll wears a sporty purple T-shirt, dark blue pleated denim skort, purple tennis shoes, and striped socks.

The collection is centered around Daisy’s Camp Gowonagin adventures, including the Daisy Davenport Camp Cabin. The cabin sleeps two dolls and includes bunk beds with pillows, blankets, and sleeping pads, an outdoor vanity with a sink and working mirror, a Camp Gowonagin flag, and more.

Additional products include a soccer set with a uniform and net, pieces inspired by Camp Gowonagin’s team activities, and camp-themed accessories. A PJ set, s’mores kit, and guitar add to Daisy’s campfire and cozy-night play.
Daisy’s story is also told through Meet Daisy Davenport , a full-length novel written by bestselling author Megan Wagner Lloyd.
RELATED New American Girl Collection is Designed by 11-Year-Old Brooke Sumpter

American Girl collaborated with experts and advisors during the development of Daisy’s story and collection, including Laurie McMurray, a former co-director of the Adventure Program at Camp Daggett; Jackie Glascock, PhD, Chief Scientific Officer at Cure SMA; and Sarah Bellish of Cure SMA’s Policy and Advocacy team, who brought personal experience attending summer camp for children with disabilities to the project.

Daisy’s story previewed this summer with Girl Scouts at the Girl Scouts Unite event in Washington, D.C. Daisy’s experience is similar to generations of Girl Scouts who explore the outdoors at more than 300 Girl Scout camps nationwide and participate in programs like Girl Scouts Love State Parks and Girl Scouts Love the Outdoors; America Girl is an official supporter of Girl Scouts of the USA.

“Our legacy began with our founder, Juliette Gordon Low — known as Daisy — and her belief in the limitless potential of every girl,” said Michelle Taylor, chief marketing officer, Girl Scouts of the USA. “We’re excited to partner with American Girl to give girls even more opportunities to believe in themselves, this time through the power of play and imagination.”

American Girl is also celebrating Daisy’s arrival with fan experiences throughout the year. bodyOriginal.text: [Bucket Mouse] has long been a fan of the various iterations of the Nintendo Game Boy. Now, he’s turned his eye to the Game Boy Advance, building an enhanced version for the console’s 25th anniversary.

There are plenty of ways to mod an existing GBA to be better than the original, but this build recreates the console from the ground up. It’s basically a brand new motherboard that replaces the original entirely, requiring only the CPU and RAM to be harvested from the original board.

It’s perfect for when you find a badly-damaged handheld that needs heavy repair, because every other part on the board can be purchased new. You can buy a nice shiny screen kit online, and even upgrade to LiPo power if so desired. The new motherboard also eliminates sound issues that are common when upgrading the screen in a classic GBA, and there’s stereo audio available on the headphone jack as standard. Battery life is also improved compared to the original.

If you’ve got a haggard old GBA in need of repair, or you just want to build the best classic handheld you can, it’s worth taking a look at this build. You might also appreciate previous works from [Bucket Mouse], like his efforts to improve the original Game Boy.

bodyOriginal.text: Damage to nuclear DNA occurs constantly, and near all of it is immediately repaired. A tiny fraction lingers, however, and over time a burden of mutational damage builds up in tissues throughout the body. It is an open question as to how large a component of degenerative aging is a direct result of this damage, under normal circumstances. High rates of mutation in individuals with disabled DNA repair mechanisms shorten life span and accelerate the onset of age-related conditions, sometimes dramatically, but that doesn't necessarily mean the DNA damage is important in aging at levels exhibited in normal individuals. The best approach to firm data is to find a way to suppress or repair mutations without affecting other mechanisms, but the life-extending interventions that are known to slow the accumulation of DNA damage also have many other beneficial effects on metabolism. As reported here, for example, calorie restriction slows the pace at which the burden of DNA damage grows over time. Calorie restriction also improves cell function and health in numerous other ways, however, producing sweeping changes in the operation of cells and systems throughout the body that are unrelated to DNA damage.

Past studies in animals have shown that a large reduction in the number of calories they consume, called caloric restriction, extends their lifespans and slows aspects of aging. But whether caloric restriction also slows the rate at which mutations occur with age had not been investigated across the genome , the complete set of genetic material present in every cell. A new study has shown that caloric restriction reduced the level of mutations across several tissues in mice that were fed 30 percent fewer calories than they would have ingested if allowed to eat freely.

The study analyzed the effect of caloric restriction on different types of genetic changes. They found that to varying degrees across tissues, it dialed down the level of substitution mutations , in which one DNA letter is swapped for another, and insertion and deletion mutations, in which one or more DNA letters are added to or missing from the genome. The study results also showed that the impact of caloric restriction varies across tissues and cell types, as well as across the genome. For example, liver cells showed a greater reduction in mutation burdens with caloric restriction than kidney or brain cells.

Surprisingly, in liver and kidney cells, the reduction in the number of mutations from caloric restriction was greatest in the least-active regions of the genome, which contain either no genes or genes not being used by a given cell. One possible explanation is that if caloric restriction reduces DNA damage across the genome, active regions of the genome would not benefit as much because those regions already repair DNA damage frequently.

articles.titleOriginal: Can we measure how fast aging is happening?
articles.summaryOriginal: Twelve candidate aging rate indicators could offer faster route to testing geroprotective drugs – and to understanding what slow aging means. The search for interventions that slow aging has an awkward experimental problem built into it: aging takes time. A mouse lifespan study can require three to four years and cost $100,000–$300,000; in humans, waiting […] The post Can we measure how fast aging

bodyOriginal.text: Twelve candidate aging rate indicators could offer faster route to testing geroprotective drugs – and to understanding what slow aging means.

The search for interventions that slow aging has an awkward experimental problem built into it: aging takes time. A mouse lifespan study can require three to four years and cost $100,000–$300,000; in humans, waiting for sufficiently convincing changes in healthspan or lifespan makes the timescale considerably less accommodating.

A new article in Frontiers in Science proposes a different way of reading the biology. Researchers from the University of Alabama at Birmingham and University of Michigan have identified 12 candidate “aging rate indicators” (ARIs) – molecular and physiological characteristics shared across mouse models in which aging has been slowed by drugs, dietary interventions or genetic mutations. Rather than estimating how much aging has accumulated, an ARI would ideally reveal whether an animal has entered a slow-aging state after an intervention.

Longevity.Technology: Geroscience has become increasingly adept at asking how old biology looks; the more consequential question for drug development is whether an intervention has actually persuaded it to age more slowly. The authors’ distinction is a useful one – aging biomarkers are closer to an odometer, recording biological miles accumulated, while an ARI is intended to behave more like a speedometer, revealing the rate of travel now. If that speedometer proves reliable, the prize is not merely faster, cheaper studies; shared changes induced by rapamycin, calorie restriction and other lifespan-extending interventions could help reveal what a slow-aging state actually is – turning measurement into a route toward mechanism, rather than simply better scorekeeping.

For now, however, these are candidate ARIs, with considerable validation required before anyone starts fitting speedometers to humans. That caution feels especially pertinent in a marketplace already rather fond of selling consumers a biological age; the authors themselves are unusually forthright about commercial aging tests and the distance between some claims and their validation. Perhaps longevity does not need another number telling us how old we supposedly are. What it needs is a rigorous way of knowing whether we have changed the trajectory – and why.

The proposal grows out of results from the National Institute on Aging-supported Interventions Testing Program (ITP), which evaluates candidate longevity interventions in genetically heterogeneous mice. Fourteen agents or combinations have significantly increased lifespan in ITP studies; eight have produced increases of at least 12% in one or both sexes, including rapamycin, acarbose, canagliflozin and 17α-estradiol.

What interests the researchers is the biological overlap. Interventions that are quite different in origin and mechanism nevertheless produce some parallel changes in signaling, metabolism, inflammation and tissue physiology.

The proposed indicators include mTORC1 activity, MEK/ERK and MEK3/p38 signaling, UCP1 in adipose tissue, inflammatory and anti-inflammatory macrophage balance, circulating irisin and GPLD1, as well as BDNF and doublecortin in the hippocampus. Importantly, no individual ARI is expected to explain aging; the working criterion is simply that it differs consistently between normal and multiple varieties of slow-aging mice [ 1 ].

Senior author Professor Richard A Miller said: “We hope aging rate indicators (ARIs) will advance the search for antiaging drugs in three ways. First, they may provide a quicker and less expensive way to select drugs that deserve testing in mice. Second, they may allow us to see which drugs can induce patterns of change in healthy people that make them more similar to slow aging mice, and therefore give clues about drugs that may slow aging in people. Lastly, the ARI panel can give us clues about the changes shared by many – perhaps all – antiaging drugs, and in this way select way targets and new drug families to work on.”

Most ARI data so far come from studies in which mice began receiving drugs or calorie restriction at four months and were assessed eight months later, using groups of just 10–20 animals of each sex. If those measurements can reliably distinguish interventions that ultimately extend lifespan from those that do not, the authors estimate experiments could run around four times faster and at roughly one-twentieth the cost of full lifespan studies.

That would make ARIs useful as a screening layer rather than a substitute for lifespan and healthspan studies – allowing researchers to discard unpromising candidates earlier and reserve longer, more expensive experiments for interventions carrying a stronger biological signal.
Optispan CEO Dr Matt Kaeberlein co-authored the new paper

“The biggest challenge in translating the biology of aging into better health is knowing whether an intervention actually affects the rate of aging,” said co-author Dr Matt Kaeberlein. “Developing and validating aging rate indicators could give us the tools to answer that question on a practical timescale, rather than waiting years or decades for lifespan outcomes. If we can do that rigorously, it will fundamentally change our ability to find interventions that extend healthy lifespan.”

There is some distance to travel. Much of the published evidence comes from a single laboratory group using one genetically heterogeneous mouse stock, making independent replication an immediate priority. Only two of the published ARIs, irisin and GPLD1, are currently measurable in plasma; developing a broader blood-based panel will be important if the approach is to move into longitudinal animal studies and eventually human trials.

The translational roadmap therefore runs through other mammals. The authors highlight companion dogs, which share human environments and develop many comparable age-related conditions, and common marmosets, whose shorter lifespans make them potentially valuable intermediary models between rodents and humans [ 1 ].
There is another encouraging wrinkle. Several ITP interventions remain effective when treatment begins relatively late in mouse life.

bodyOriginal.alt: Aging research conducted in mice has already led to the discovery and development of several drugs, some of which are already in human clinical trial, but Austad is far from convinced that the positive results seen in mice will translate into human longevity benefits.

bodyOriginal.text: Professor Steven Austad is lead author on the new paper

“The surprising discovery in mice that many effective antiaging drugs remain fully active even when started in late adulthood suggests that similar therapies could perhaps benefit people in middle age, which is an exciting possibility,” said lead author Professor Steven Austad.

“ARIs could play a pivotal role in advancing these preventative therapies, culminating – eventually – in human clinical trials that can be completed in far shorter timeframes to speed access to new antiaging drugs.”

The authors are deliberately cautious about equating correlation with measurement: as they put it, “currently we have no way to measure biological age or biological aging rate.” ARIs will have to earn their status by predicting outcomes that matter.

If they do, the shift could be subtle but important. Geroscience would have something more useful than another estimate of biological age: an experimentally testable signal that biology has changed direction. The speedometer still needs calibrating; knowing where the accelerator and brake are would be more interesting still.

bodyOriginal.text: A Matti Suuronen Futuro House has been manufactured for the first time in decades and decked out by Finnish design brand Marimekko for Helsinki Design Week .
The famously flying-saucer-like structure recently landed in Kaisaniemi Botanical Gardens as part of the Finnish capital's annual design festival .
Initially conceived as a transportable ski cabin by Finnish architect Matti Suuronen in 1968, the Futuro House is among the most distinctive emblems of space-age architecture.

bodyOriginal.alt: Futuro House at Helsinki Design Week 2026

bodyOriginal.text: The first new Futuro House for decades made an appearance at Helsinki Design Week. Photo by Justus Hirvi Prefrabricated in fibreglass-reinforced plastic, it was once described by British critic Justin McGuirk as "the closest housing ever came to product design".
Despite being intended for mass production, fewer than 100 were made worldwide. Manufacture ceased shortly after the 1973 oil crisis, which sent the price of plastic rocketing.
Around 60 are estimated to still be in existence, scattered across the globe in varying states of repair.

That number became one greater recently for the first time in decades, thanks to a project that began in 2024 when Dutch-American preservationist architect Jan van Dijs was alerted by a friend and client to an unusual post on Facebook.
An executive at a Finnish materials firm, Exel Composites, was selling the original Futuro moulds.
"How fascinating if we could actually do this"
At this point, Van Dijs, who has spent much of his career restoring mid-century houses in California , was only vaguely familiar with the Futuro Houses.
"I dug in a little bit, I started to learn about the history," he told Dezeen. "And I start to realise that it's something of a fascinating story."

"And I really had my doubts that all the pieces were there, that they could be restored, so I tried to keep all of that in check," he added. "But I certainly had started to make an emotional connection to how fascinating this could be if we could actually do this."
Twenty Futuro Houses had been fabricated in its native Finland originally, by plastics company PolyKem.

Exel had acquired PolyKem's assets, including the Futuro moulds, after the fabricator went bankrupt in the early 1990s – a difficult period for Suuronen that reportedly culminated in him and his wife losing their home.

bodyOriginal.alt: Futuro moulds

bodyOriginal.text: The moulds were in a sorry state when van Dijs first saw them. Photo by Jan van Dijs In the decades since production stopped, the moulds had been periodically moved between various forms of storage without a purpose.
Suuronen died in 2013, and so once hooked on the Futuro story, Van Dijs spent several months trying to engage with the architect's family.

"I couldn't just buy the moulds and build this thing – I needed to have a license, and I needed to have their support," he said. "The reality was, unless I could do that, there was no future for this project."
The Suuronens were hesitant, having been contacted several times over the years about poorly thought-through schemes on a similar theme.
But eventually they were persuaded with help from the Exel man, Jyrki Aho, who died a short while later.
When Van Dijs flew out to see the moulds in May 2025, they were languishing in a field and nearly 60 years old.
"The exterior of the moulds looked like hell," he remembered. "I mean, there was grass growing out of them and moss covering them, and it looked really bad."

Nevertheless, the decision was made to proceed, and Van Dijs worked with Finnish plastic fabrication company Ekin Muovi to restore the moulds and recast the panels with the aim of producing a faithful reconstruction of Suuronen's design.

bodyOriginal.alt: Futuro House moulds

bodyOriginal.text: The pieces had been drifting into decay since the 1970s. Photo by Jan van Dijs Even the same paint colours were used, having been matched from scraps that remained on the moulds.
It was a step into the unknown for Van Dijs, and he admits the process was trickier than he had anticipated.

While today plastic moulding uses two tessellating pieces – one to pour the cast into and one to press over it to squeeze out all the air – Suuronen's are one-part moulds, meaning air bubbles must be eliminated manually.
"It's all hand labour," said Van Dijs. "Nobody does it like that anymore."
Casting a single panel therefore took days instead of hours and was very labour-intensive – "no doubt a large contributor to the problems faced by the Futuro in the 1970s", Van Dijs suggests.

bodyOriginal.alt: Futuro House fabrication

bodyOriginal.text: Casting the new Futuro panels was a painstaking process. Photo by Jan van Dijs There were pleasant surprises as well, however. Unexpectedly, the moulds being sold by Exel included furniture designs by Suuronen, which have also been reproduced as part of the project.
They include built-in lounge chairs, a dining table, and the Orbit chair.

The fabrication process took five months, including some mishaps along the way. Including the restoration of the moulds, Van Dijs estimates the project has cost around 450,000 Euros, though he hopes further Futuros would cost less than 300,000.

In late June of this year, the 21st Futuro House to be made in its native country was completed, ready to be transported in several pieces for reassembly at its temporary home on the Kaisaniemi lawns.

bodyOriginal.alt: Half-built Futuro House

bodyOriginal.text: The new Futuro was manufactured in five months, completing in late June. Photo by Jan van Dijs For the Helsinki Design Week installation, Marimekko was invited to create an interior for the new Futuro House.
It opted to divide the open space into three areas – one for lounging and sleeping, one for eating and working, and a kitchenette.
"It was really important to sort of create a proposal for future ways of living," Marimekko creative director Rebekka Bay told Dezeen.

"That sounds like a big, grand statement, but we were really just intrigued by how we would live in the Futuro House today. I think there is a real trend for downscaling, and we felt that the Futuro House is sort of speaking to that."

bodyOriginal.alt: Marimekko installation at Helsinki Design Week 2026

bodyOriginal.text: Marimekko wanted its Futuro installation to feel "tactile, lived-in". Photo by Justus Hirvi Marimekko products were displayed on perspex shelving units that double as transparent room dividers, while stripy prints created for the brand during a residency by Danish textile artist Vibeke Rohland were used to upholster the furniture.
"It would have been obvious for us, of course, to go back to our archives and find prints that were designed in 1968 when the house was also designed," said Bay.

"But we wanted to take the opposite route and propose something that had been created today. We convey certain images when we speak to the future, but we wanted our proposal to be sort of tactile, lived-in, friendlier, and were therefore intrigued to use brand new textile designs."
With design week over, discussions about the structure's future are now ongoing, though Van Dijs said his preference is for it to remain on public display in Finland.

bodyOriginal.alt: Marimekko Futuro House installation

bodyOriginal.text: The brand's products were displayed on transparent shelving units. Photo by Justus Hirvi "I hope it will move somewhere into the countryside and someone will be using it as their summer cabin," said Bay. "I think that would be wonderful."
Van Dijs also plans to produce new Futuro Houses to order – but the run will be limited.
"Casting moulds are just like the plates for a print; they are designed for a limited number of editions," he said.
"I think the original moulds were probably near the end of their lifespan when production stopped. Through a significant effort we were able to extend their life, but not forever."

Read: "What if houses were designed like bikes?" He estimates that the restored moulds will support producing between four and six new Futuros. After that the moulds will be destroyed, and, in Van Dijs's words, "that will be the end of the original Futuros".
In his design, Suuronen focused on making the Futuro House quick to assemble, quick to heat and suitable for difficult terrains.
But it is also cramped, tricky to transport and dreadfully insulated, leaving it without an obvious practical use in 2026.

bodyOriginal.alt: Futuro House at Helsinki Design Week

bodyOriginal.text: Plans for the Futuro's next home are still being finalised. Photo by Justus Hirvi Nevertheless, Van Dijs is adamant that Suuronen's creation is more than mere whimsy.
"I would love to leave my home every day and go to my Futuro office, a small apartment, yoga studio, architectural book store," he suggested.

He regards the Futuro as an important touchstone for radical post-war optimism and creativity – the same conditions from which Marimekko was born in 1951 – and sees his project as a reigniting of that spirit.
"I think the Futuro should be considered an icon of Finnish design, which was not the case when it was originally produced," he said.
"This project allows us to see the Futuro as Matti Suuronen envisioned it – I think that's important."

bodyOriginal.text: Promotion: in a time of dopamine design and AI tools , a group of design industry professionals at an Arca talk discussed what role colour is playing in the contemporary American home.
Colours such as olive greens and a shade called Black Martini are in, according to Tony Piloseno, owner of Orlando-based company Tonester Paints .
Piloseno joined interior designers Kati Curtis and Tamara Feldman for a conversation at Mexican stone company Arca' s showroom in Miami, moderated by Dezeen US editor Ben Dreith.
And while the panellists agreed that rich, dark colours are in at the moment, the most important element of contemporary colour usage is about experience and reevaluating how people choose colour.

bodyOriginal.alt: Arca Wynwood

bodyOriginal.text: Arca and Dezeen hosted a talk at the Mexican stone company's Wynwood Miami showroom "I use tons of colour in my work, but what I'm thinking about, more so than trends, is how are we using colour?" said Curtis. "Are we using colour as an applied element, or is colour actually architecture?"
Both Curtis and Feldman referenced the work of Mexican modernist architect Luis Barragán in their framing of colour as more than a trendy accent.

"The term colour blocking has always bothered me because I feel like it's an accent – it's like putting wallpaper on one wall," continued Curtis. "It feels to me like you ran out of money, and you just went with that."

bodyOriginal.alt: Dezeen pane

bodyOriginal.text: The panellists included (from left) Ben Dreith, Tamara Feldman, Kati Curtis and Tony Piloseno An expanded conception of colour utilises light, texture, and the aim should be to envelop whoever is in a space. The panellists noted how the presence of tinted glass in Miami makes this even more important.
This, for Feldman, means that the whole of an interior – including light – and all the way through to the artwork on the walls should work together.
"I don't think it's just about a colour and a wall," she said. "I think it's the whole concept together."

Feldman is currently designing a coffee pavilion for the Institute of Contemporary Art in Miami, where she has used mirrors and Arca's Umbria-fabricate tiles to create a sculptural work in the institution's gardens.

bodyOriginal.alt: Tony Piloseno with microphone

bodyOriginal.text: Piloseno spoke on contemporary colour trends and specifying techniques The idea that colour should envelop and create an emotional response has become a hot topic recently, with the emerging trend of so-called "dopamine design" seeing spaces covered in bright colours and mish-mashed patterns to stimulate the mind.

The panellists agreed that colour can work to make you feel at ease, comfortable or inspired, but that this is more related to individual preference and experience than any set configuration or style.

"Does the room look really cool on TikTok, then you hate it 15 minutes later because you threw it in there to try to create this cool picture?" asked Curtis. "It can definitely go in the wrong direction too if you don't know what you're doing."

bodyOriginal.alt: Tamara Feldman

bodyOriginal.text: The panellists agreed on the usefulness of AI but highlighted the personal aspects of colour selection and design Piloseno added that dark colours that wash over you can have a positive effect as well.
"There is a direct emotional impact that colour has, especially with these darker colours," he said.

The panellists also addressed AI in design, and how choosing a colour scheme can be risky. For example, once you apply the paint or veneer, it takes a significant amount of work to pivot in a different direction.
Visualisation tools have existed for years, but Curtis said that generative AI has allowed her to show clients what a space might look like more easily before they commit.

"Even if it's not an accurate representation of exactly what the colour is going to be, I think it's very helpful in giving clients an idea of the overall room rather than just testing a sample," said Curtis.
"What AI and just any kind of colour visualiser tool will help with is seeing the specific colour vertically or how it's going to look on the ceiling with specific shadows," added Piloseno.
Ultimately, though, the panellists agreed that the pursuit of colour, and whatever downstream emotional effects, requires a human touch.
"I think the whole process of selecting colours is very personal," said Piloseno. "You shouldn't have AI guide you to these specific colours."

bodyOriginal.alt: Arca showroom Dezeen talk

bodyOriginal.text: The event brought out a large crowd of Miami professionals The speakers added that personal relationships and understanding the emotions of clients are paramount.
Colour choices often represent this dynamic more than other aspects of design. If a designer is going to understand what will engage the mind, they need to know the mind in question.
"What we do is really part therapy, part design," said Feldman.

Technology underwrites the process while the person guides the choices on the table. And while neuroscience has created new streams for engaging with design schemes, Curtis said that the foundations remain as important as ever.
"As long as you stick with those fundamental elements that we all know, we can mix all of those things in a really beautiful way," added Feldman. "That's going to make everybody's dopamine work."

bodyOriginal.text: A pasta-shaped daybed and speakers that resemble Saturn's rings are among the products on display at Contemporary Design Selections at this year's Lake Como Design Festival .

The eighth edition of the Contemporary Design Selections show, curated by Giovanna Massoni , follows the festival theme of Borders, encouraging participating designers, architects and makers to consider boundaries in design.
The theme could be interpreted through materiality, form, function or design's relation to other disciplines, while the open call also highlighted the social and political elements of the industry.
The exhibition is located at Villa Saporiti, which marks the first public showcase in the neoclassical building, and displays 57 projects by designers and studios from 30 countries.
The showcase features furniture, lighting, functional objects and textiles selected by Massoni across 10 rooms in the villa and its outdoor spaces.
Read on for seven design pieces that caught our attention:

bodyOriginal.text: Belgium-based Studio Bjorn Verlinde spotlighted its minimal Fur seating and side table collection at the exhibition.
Designed for restless people, the series features an unconventional backless rocking chair with a curved aluminium base that allows the user to gently lean back.
A contrasting seat made from brown leather sits atop the base of the chair, which is mirrored by the surface of the accompanying table.

bodyOriginal.alt: Photo of light by Massimo Rigaglia

bodyOriginal.text: Massimo Rigaglia , a Milan-based artist and designer, created the Lights in Tension light collection from strips of flexible bamboo held in place by leather cords.

bodyOriginal.text: BR Collection by Studio Alessandra Hofmann
These coffee tables by Basel-based Studio Alessandra Hofmann were informed by brutalist architecture.
The cube-shaped blocks of travertine are intersected with rectangular slabs of handmade cast glass, creating two levels to the tabletop.
The designer took an experimental approach to working with natural materials, embracing reactions created in the design process such as bubbles in the glass and open pores in the travertine.

bodyOriginal.text: This 10-metre-long wool rug by textile studio The Happy Few was designed to reflect the experience of walking down the street, with rectangular woven blocks resembling street tiles.

articles.titleOriginal: The Most Powerful Economic Productivity Lever of All Time
articles.summaryOriginal: A great deal of advocacy for the development of therapies to slow and reverse aging has moved on from a focus on reducing suffering. bodyOriginal.text: A great deal of advocacy for the development of therapies to slow and reverse aging has moved on from a focus on reducing suffering. That the majority of the arguments now focus on economic productivity and reduced entitlement costs reflects a broad and possibly quite correct cynicism about what motivates the politicians, wealthy political influencers, and bureaucrats who collectively control the largest flows of funding and support in our societies. Private funding for research and development focused on longevity remains very motivated by the potential reduced suffering, and indeed the potential to reduce one's own personal suffering in the years ahead. However, the longevity industry of the recent past, and for the near future, exists in a state of tension as it attempts to make the transition from a privately supported new venture to an established field supported by the full panoply of state controlled medical systems - to be as openly and comprehensively backed by governments as cancer research and development.

Most advocates these days appear to believe that the way to make this happen is to exploit the high level of anxiety in the ruling classes of much of the world that centers around the demographic transition to ever increasing numbers of older people, and the costs of old age. The governments of the world have largely chosen to exert a great deal of control over the development and provision of medicine, to the point of it becoming an expense for them, a burden much akin to the mess that was made of pension entitlements, the creation of large enough promises of future expenditure to financially ruin the systems created to manage them. Treatments for aging are a deus ex machina that will save the system, or that is the hope being pushed into government circles by advocates attempting to achieve greater support for the development of longevity therapeutics. The realpolitik always seems somewhat shabby in full daylight when it departs utterly from the considerations of what aging does to an individual, physically and mentally. The true reason to build therapies to treat aging is because this offers the strong possibility of a very sizable reduction in human suffering and death, not because it can prop up dysfunction systems of governance.
The longevity dividend: Why governments and markets must catch up

'How much' often matters less than 'how fast'. Financial systems might comfortably accommodate a decade increase in life expectancy if it emerges gradually over half a century, but could they accommodate the same increase within 5 years? Economies are built to absorb gradual change and are much less comfortable with discontinuities. Human longevity may be approaching that kind of discontinuity . The latest scientific advances point to the emergence of what we have termed 'system-level' therapeutics capable of bringing about rapid, non-linear changes in both healthspan and lifespan trajectories, challenging the incremental paradigms that underpin current economic and demographic forecasting models. If they do, governments, healthcare systems, insurers and pension funds will have to respond to a break with history, not a continuation of it.

Public debate often treats longevity as a cost curve. That is only half the ledger. In an era of demographic ageing and stagnant economic growth forecasts, one overlooked truth is emerging: longevity science may be the most powerful economic productivity lever of all time. Governments spend billions annually on education, digital transformation and industrial innovation - all in the name of boosting national productivity. Yet few acknowledge that the single largest drag on workforce participation is declining health in midlife and beyond due to ageing. In the United States, the direct costs of chronic health conditions total around $1.1 trillion - equivalent to 5.8% of US gross domestic product (GDP). When indirect costs of lost economic productivity are included, the total costs of chronic diseases in the United States increase to $3.7 trillion - in other words, they equate to almost 20% of the US GDP.

The economic argument for longevity research is clear: targeting the root causes of ageing is not just a healthcare imperative, it is set to become a non-negotiable economic strategy. Governments should treat it as such, allocating funding accordingly and incentivising translational research , clinical trials, and public-private partnerships in this field. In the 20th century, public investment in antibiotics and vaccines changed the world. In the 21st century, ageing biology has the potential to do the same.
