bodyOriginal.text: Company bets that AI-assisted analysis and a leaner trial design can get PrimeC to patients years sooner than the usual approval path.

Most people diagnosed with ALS don’t live past three years. Most drugs aiming to treat it spend longer than that just getting through a single confirmatory trial. That mismatch is the entire problem NeuroSense Therapeutics is trying to solve.

Late last month, the Cambridge, Massachusetts-based biotech announced it’s scrapping the traditional single-trial approach for its lead ALS candidate, PrimeC, in favor of three shorter, narrower studies. Each is designed to answer one specific question instead of trying to prove everything at once inside a single, years-long trial [ 1 ].

“One of the hardest constraints in ALS is not scientific; it is that the standard development path takes longer than patients have,” said Alon Ben-Noon, NeuroSense’s co-founder and CEO. “We have asked a straightforward question: what is the shortest reasonable route from the data we already hold to a therapy people can actually receive? This plan is our answer. It is faster, it costs less and it produces a stronger package, pharmacology, comparative clinical context and a pivotal dataset, than the single-trial approach would have.”

PrimeC pairs two already-approved drugs, ciprofloxacin, an antibiotic and celecoxib, an anti-inflammatory, into a single extended-release formulation. The idea isn’t novel chemistry so much as novel packaging: combine two known drugs to hit several of ALS’s suspected drivers simultaneously – nervous-system inflammation, iron accumulation in neurons and RNA regulation gone haywire – rather than betting everything on one mechanism the way most single-molecule drugs do.

The first piece of the plan is almost entirely desk work. NeuroSense already has pharmacokinetic data showing that PrimeC’s specific formulation produces a different, synchronized absorption pattern than simply taking the two component drugs side by side.

Rather than run a new trial to prove that, the company is applying AI-based modeling to data it already collected, hunting for a sharper, more defensible read on how big that difference actually is and how consistently it shows up across patients. It’s less a discovery than an extraction, pulling a stronger claim out of a file the company already owns.

The second study is the riskier bet. NeuroSense plans to run PrimeC head-to-head against edaravone, an ALS drug already on the market. Most ALS trials compare a candidate against a placebo, which is the safer route; there’s nowhere to hide the results if a placebo comparison goes badly, but there’s also less to gain. A direct win against an established competitor would hand NeuroSense something no placebo trial can: proof PrimeC beats what doctors are already prescribing. That’s the kind of evidence insurers and physicians weigh when deciding what to cover and prescribe.

Piece three reshapes PARAGON, the Phase 3 trial NeuroSense already has FDA clearance to run. The redesigned version would be smaller, shorter, and enroll patients earlier in their disease course, when meaningful decline is easier to detect over a compressed timeline. NeuroSense says it intends to ask the FDA directly whether existing data could support full approval outright, or whether accelerated approval, with a confirmatory study required afterward, is the more realistic path.

There’s also a second front open in Canada. NeuroSense has finished the pre-submission process with Health Canada and is targeting a formal filing by December, a track that could put PrimeC in Canadian patients’ hands before the US process wraps up.

Underneath the trial mechanics, NeuroSense is testing something broader: whether AI-assisted analysis of data a company already has, paired with a leaner trial architecture, can shrink the distance between “we have promising evidence” and “patients can access this,” without cutting corners on rigor to get there.

For neurodegenerative disease specifically, where biological aging and disease progression run on the same clock, that kind of speed isn’t a nice-to-have. It’s the line between a therapy reaching someone in time to preserve years of function and reaching them after those years are already gone.

None of it is locked in yet. The FDA hasn’t signed off on the redesigned pivotal trial, and a head-to-head study against an approved competitor carries real reputational downside if PrimeC comes up short. However, the underlying argument – that the industry’s default trial timeline is itself an obstacle to treating aging-related disease, however sound the science behind a drug turns out to be – is one more companies working in this space are likely to test in the next few years.

bodyOriginal.text: Durham University spinout Magnitude Biosciences raises $1.3 million to scale a platform that screens drugs in living worms, not petri dishes.

There’s a particular kind of worm, about a millimeter long, that’s quietly become one of the most useful tools in aging research. C elegans has been a lab staple for decades because it shares a surprising number of genes and biological pathways with humans, and because researchers can watch its entire lifespan play out in a matter of weeks rather than years. A UK company built around exactly that idea, Magnitude Biosciences , just secured fresh funding to scale up what it’s doing with them.

The company, a contract research organization and Durham University spinout based in Sedgefield, has raised $1.3 million (£1.3 million) to accelerate the commercialization of VivoScan, its proprietary high-throughput screening platform. What makes VivoScan different from standard drug screening is right there in the name: it’s happening in a whole living organism, not in isolated cells or molecules in a dish.

Conventional high-throughput screening typically measures a handful of molecular or cellular endpoints. VivoScan instead uses hundreds of nematode worms at a time, combined with imaging, machine learning, and automation, to capture a much richer picture of how a compound actually behaves across a whole organism’s biology. The company says it can generate detailed, whole-organism data in weeks, compared to the years that similar work can take using traditional models.

It sounds like an odd pitch until you consider how much drug development currently fails. Compounds routinely look promising in isolated cells, then fail once tested in a full organism, because biology doesn’t work in isolated pieces. A platform that captures whole-organism responses earlier in the process, rather than discovering the problem years and millions of dollars later, has an obvious appeal to pharmaceutical companies trying to cut both cost and failure rates.

“Our ambition is to become the first company to provide a platform to screen millions of compounds in a whole organism. This investment in VivoScan gives us the opportunity to turn that ambition into reality and fundamentally change the scale and speed at which drug discovery can be done,” said Dr Fozia Saleem, CEO of Magnitude Biosciences. “We are building a platform that can move beyond simply screening more compounds. VivoScan generates rich, whole organism biological data that can help researchers understand how potential therapies affect health, aging and disease.”

Saleem noted that making data generation faster and more cost-effective would enable them to help pharmaceutical and biotechnology companies identify better drug candidates earlier, which would ultimately accelerate the development of new treatments.

Northstar Ventures led the round, drawing on the North East Spinout Inspire Fund, the North East Innovation Fund, and the Northstar EIS Growth Fund, alongside investment from Maven’s regional funds and a group of new angel investors. The round also unlocked a further $217,000 grant (£217,000) through the Innovate UK Investor Partnership. It’s a fairly regional story in that sense, a company built on North East England’s university research ecosystem, funded largely by the same ecosystem’s investment infrastructure.

Magnitude has already delivered more than 120 projects for clients working across drug discovery, health and nutrition, and aging biology specifically, using its patented WormGazer technology alongside VivoScan. That last category is where the company’s ambitions and the longevity field’s needs line up most directly.

Aging research has a specific, stubborn problem: almost nothing about aging shows up quickly. A compound meant to extend healthspan can’t easily be tested the way a painkiller can, because the whole point is watching what happens over a long stretch of time, and mice alone take two to three years to show meaningful lifespan data. C elegans , with a lifespan measured in weeks, lets researchers run that same kind of longitudinal test dramatically faster, then flag the most promising candidates for further testing in mammals.

That’s precisely the gap Magnitude is aiming at. As the company put it in its own announcement, the goal is to help “accelerate the development of new drugs designed to extend the healthspan of our aging population.” Whether VivoScan becomes the industry-standard bridge between petri-dish chemistry and full clinical trials is still an open question, but the underlying bet, that screening in a living, aging organism beats screening in isolated cells, is one a growing share of the field seems to agree with.

bodyOriginal.text: Yale-led analysis harmonized 51 studies under one standardized pipeline, and senolytics came out looking shaky.

Send in a vial of blood, get back a number, skip the decades of waiting it used to take to know if something is actually slowing your aging. That’s the pitch behind epigenetic aging clocks, and it’s a big part of why direct-to-consumer biological age testing has grown into its own industry over the past few years. A new study just put that pitch under harsher scrutiny than it usually gets.

Researchers at Yale University, publishing in Nature Medicine on 21 August, pooled 51 published and private human intervention studies (3,128 blood samples in total) and ran each through the same standardized pipeline, calculating 16 widely used epigenetic clocks plus 94 additional DNA methylation biomarkers for each dataset [ 1 ]. Different studies have historically processed data differently, making honest comparisons across the field nearly impossible. This is one of the first attempts to fix that.

The results: 19 of the 51 interventions produced a statistically significant decrease in epigenetic age. After correcting for the false-positive risk that comes with testing so many biomarkers at once, that number dropped to 13. Five interventions actually increased epigenetic age. The remaining 26, a bit more than half the studies included, showed no significant movement either way.
Pick one of these already-published interventions at random, in other words, and the odds don’t favor it doing anything measurable at all.

The sharpest finding concerns senolytics, drugs designed to clear out senescent cells, the aged cells that stop dividing but keep pumping out inflammatory signals that damage the tissue around them. Senolytics also happen to be one of the most heavily marketed ideas in consumer longevity right now.

Five senolytic studies made it into the analysis, and the results didn’t line up. Different biomarkers moved in opposite directions within the same study. The same biomarker sometimes moved in opposite directions across separate studies of the same intervention. To separate real signal from noise, the researchers set two bars: a genuine effect should move biomarkers of the same generation, in the same direction and magnitude, within a single study, and a repeat study of the same intervention should reproduce that movement. Senolytics cleared neither one.

Only two interventions in the entire dataset cleared both bars. Anti-TNF therapies, anti-inflammatory drugs used for rheumatoid arthritis and inflammatory bowel disease, shifted nearly all second-generation biomarkers by comparable amounts across multiple independent studies.

Two separate Mediterranean diet protocols, tested in different healthy cohorts, decreased overlapping sets of biomarkers in ways that matched each other. As a category, drugs produced significantly bigger effects than either lifestyle changes or supplements.

There’s a finding here that matters just as much for anyone shopping for a consumer test: the clocks aren’t interchangeable. Older, first-generation clocks, including the original Horvath and Hannum measures, moved sporadically with no consistent pattern. The researchers found that a meaningful chunk of what the Horvath clock registers may just be random biological noise, not something an intervention could plausibly move.

Newer, second-generation clocks built for reliability did better. DunedinPACE, designed to track the pace of aging rather than accumulated age, decreased significantly in 16 interventions and increased in just one, the largest effect size anywhere in the analysis.

A related measure called PCGrimAge produced the strongest statistical evidence overall. Different clocks also suited different interventions better than others: DunedinPACE stood out for lifestyle changes, GrimAgeV2 for drugs.

The paper is unusually direct about its own limits. A biomarker responding to an intervention, the authors write, is a prerequisite for eventually using it as a shortcut for real health outcomes, not proof that it already works as one. A clock moving isn’t the same thing as a person becoming biologically younger, and the study can’t say whether the short-term shifts it measured actually translate into a longer or healthier life down the road.

One disclosure worth flagging: several authors are affiliated with TruDiagnostic , a commercial epigenetic testing company that supplied some of the private datasets and controls the algorithms behind two of the clocks analyzed. The paper discloses the relationship directly.

For a longevity field that has leaned hard on the promise of a fast blood-test answer, this study is a useful gut check. It doesn’t say biological age testing is worthless, and it doesn’t say every anti-aging product on the market is snake oil. It says the honest answer to “is this working,” for most products people are already paying for, is that nobody has rigorously checked yet. Until someone does, a lower number on a test report isn’t the same thing as more years or better years, actually gained.

bodyOriginal.text: Our new report maps more than 3,000 therapeutic assets, tracing how money, pipelines and pharma appetite are now moving in step.

Longevity biotech could become a $617 billion annual global market by 2045, according to a new Longevity.Technology report that maps the investment, clinical and regulatory forces moving therapies targeting the biology of aging towards mainstream medicine.

The Longevity Biotech Report , released today and supported by MuseCell Innovations , draws on our proprietary DLT dataset covering more than 781 biotech companies and 3,580 therapeutic assets globally; 3,036 assets were individually modeled in its bottom-up pipeline valuation. The analysis estimates $230 billion in risk-adjusted peak annual sales from therapies pursuing existing disease indications under current regulatory pathways – before attributing additional value to future gerotherapeutic approvals.

Longevity.Technology: The headline numbers are large, but the more interesting story may be what is happening underneath them. Longevity biotech no longer needs to wait for aging to become a recognized indication; therapies targeting its biology can reach patients through metabolic, cardiovascular, neurological and other familiar disease pathways, accumulating evidence – and value – as they go. The irony is that prevention, ostensibly the point of geroscience, remains one of the smallest parts of the modeled market; science tells us to intervene upstream, while healthcare systems remain considerably better equipped to pay us once something has gone wrong.

What feels significant now is convergence. Capital is concentrating, pipelines are maturing, pharma is engaging and the regulatory conversation is shifting; these forces are moving at different speeds, but increasingly in the same direction. Regenerative medicine takes that trajectory a step further – from modifying the processes that drive age-related disease towards restoring damaged or depleted biology, with platform technologies potentially spanning tissues, indications and applications.

None of this makes the future market inevitable; biology has never shown much respect for a spreadsheet. But longevity biotech is beginning to build routes to patients and commercial validation before the regulatory destination is fully mapped – and markets have a habit of arriving before we have quite decided what to call them.

Investment reached $18.4 billion in 2025, up from $4.7 billion in 2024, with a further $12.1 billion invested during 2026 to date. The shape of that funding is changing too: fewer, larger deals are concentrating capital around selected companies and platforms rather than distributing it evenly across the sector.

Phil Newman, Founder and CEO of Longevity.Technology, said: “The significance of this report is not simply the size of the market we project; it is that we can now trace how we get there, asset by asset. Longevity biotech is becoming measurable through the same clinical, regulatory and commercial signals used to assess the wider pharmaceutical industry.”

That assessment includes more than 1,000 programs already in human trials. Under the report’s model, the existing pipeline could generate around $230 billion in risk-adjusted peak annual sales through established disease indications; formal recognition of a gerotherapeutic pathway, modeled from around 2035, could eventually add another $173 billion annually from broader longevity applications.

The $617 billion projection is a separate top-down model, based on assumptions including global adoption, prevention beginning from age 45, pricing broadly comparable with current GLP-1 therapies, 35% peak uptake and a ten-year diffusion period.

The numbers come with caveats. Gerotherapeutics remain without a dedicated FDA or EMA regulatory category and questions around validated aging biomarkers, meaningful endpoints and trial design are unresolved.

Dr Nir Barzilai, Director of the Institute of Aging Research at Albert Einstein College of Medicine and a reviewer of the report, captures the opportunity succinctly: “The promise of geroscience is that we treat our health rather than our disease.”
Clinical evidence will determine how much of that promise survives contact with patients.

That challenge becomes particularly interesting for regenerative medicine. The report separates conventional drug-like assets from regenerative platforms, which carry greater manufacturing and delivery complexity but can potentially apply a validated cell or tissue technology across multiple diseases and clinical pathways.

(L–R:) Dr Dominik Duscher (President and CEO of MuseCell Innovations), Phil Newman (Founder and CEO of Longevity.Technology) and Dr Nir Barzilai (Director of the Institute of Aging Research at Albert Einstein College of Medicine)

MuseCell Innovations, which supported the report, provides one example through its development of Dezawa Muse Cells – endogenous, stress-tolerant cells being investigated as an allogeneic regenerative platform across several indications. Its accompanying report spotlight examines their damage-directed homing, differentiation and potential applications spanning acute injury and chronic tissue decline.

For Dr Dominik Duscher, President and CEO of MuseCell Innovations , regenerative medicine brings something distinct to the longevity toolkit. As he writes in the report ’s foreword: “Regenerative medicine brings a distinct objective to longevity research: restoring tissue function where aging and disease have impaired the body’s capacity for repair.”

That distinction matters as the field moves beyond slowing or modifying the processes associated with age-related disease towards asking whether lost function can be restored. Duscher is careful, however, about what follows from platform potential: each application still requires evidence of meaningful benefit in the patients concerned.

A $617 billion forecast deserves interrogation, not reverence. The more immediate question is whether the scientific, clinical and regulatory pieces continue to move together; if they do, longevity biotech will be shaped not by one defining drug or modality, but by the rather less cinematic business of accumulating evidence.

bodyOriginal.text: At a Munich cardiology congress, a Korean startup’s ring-shaped monitor drew crowds asking how fast they could buy in bulk.

Ask any startup founder what a good trade show looks like, and most will tell you it is not applause; it is people asking about volume pricing. That is roughly what happened to Sky Labs at the European Society of Cardiology’s 2026 congress in Munich recently, where visitors to the company’s booth kept circling back with a version of the same question: could they buy the company’s blood pressure ring in batches of 100 or 200 units?

Sky Labs makes CART BP pro, a ring worn on the finger that measures blood pressure continuously, without a cuff, without an arm sleeve, without any of the paraphernalia that has made ambulatory blood pressure monitoring, the gold-standard way to catch dangerous swings a single office reading misses, something most patients only tolerate for a day or two at most.

“The discussions we had already been having with global pharmaceutical companies and other global companies have advanced quite a lot,” said Sky Labs CEO Lee Byung-hwan, speaking to Korea Biomedical Review at the congress [ 1 ]. “Based on the clinical evidence we have built, conversations have become easier, and I think some of these projects could progress faster than we originally expected.”

The company’s confidence traces back to home turf. CART BP pro has already built up a real prescribing track record in Korea, where it earned reimbursement and has since accumulated what Lee describes as a substantial volume of prescriptions in a relatively short window. That real-world data trail, generated even before reimbursement kicked in, is now the evidence base Sky Labs is exporting to the rest of the world.

It also helped move a domestic medical society. The Korean Society of Hypertension this year recommended the use of validated cuffless blood pressure devices, a step Lee called unusually fast by the standards of clinical guideline development, which typically takes years to catch up to new technology. “Even if it does not go all the way into a guideline immediately, a position paper or statement can have a very significant impact,” he said.
Selling into Europe without selling directly

Sky Labs is not handling European retail sales itself. Instead, it has partnered with the German distributor IEM , which received its first shipments earlier this year and expects devices to reach the market in the back half of 2026. Interest at ESC 2026 suggests that rollout could accelerate faster than planned, and feedback IEM’s own distribution partners gave after trying the device firsthand has reportedly been encouraging.

Market entry will not look identical everywhere. In some countries, ambulatory monitoring is already available outside public reimbursement systems, letting private clinics adopt it quickly. In others, adoption hinges on securing formal reimbursement, a process Lee says is moving faster than the company initially expected, with the United Kingdom held up as a case where a substantial private healthcare market can carry early commercial adoption while public reimbursement talks continue in parallel.

The company has already brought on a contract research organization to run a U.S. clinical study that could start as soon as next month, aiming to wrap enrollment in the first half of next year and move through the FDA’s review process in the back half.

Sky Labs is pursuing the FDA’s de novo pathway, generally reserved for novel device categories without an existing predicate, and Lee said the company does not currently view that route as unusually difficult given the clinical evidence already in hand.

Longer term, Sky Labs wants CART BP pro to be a beachhead rather than the destination. The company is developing a broader family of ring-based sensors, including CART ON, CART O2 and CART VITAL, aimed at other physiological signals, part of a bet that healthcare monitoring is migrating out of hospitals and into whatever a patient is already wearing.

That migration matters more than it might first appear for anyone tracking healthy aging. Hypertension is one of the single biggest modifiable drivers of cardiovascular disease, stroke and cognitive decline, and yet a huge share of it goes undetected or poorly controlled precisely because office readings capture a single snapshot rather than the fuller pattern of a person’s day.

A device unobtrusive enough that someone will actually wear it for weeks, not just the standard 24-hour monitoring window, could catch the white-coat and masked hypertension that conventional cuffs miss entirely, and catch it early enough for it to matter.

Lee is careful not to oversell the moment. Broader market conditions have made the company’s path to an IPO tougher than once expected, he acknowledged, even as he insisted the underlying growth strategy has not changed.
“The fundamental point is whether the company is heading in the right direction and whether it can show that it is actually getting there,” he said. “We believe we are continuing on that path.”

bodyOriginal.text: Inspired by shapes and movement found in nature, Pablo Luna Studio conceives of hospitality spaces, wellness retreats, and homes that sympathize with their surroundings. Rather than creating a barrier between outside and inside, the airy structures welcome foliage and the natural landscape into the overall experience, blurring the boundary between structure and environment.

The firm, based in Ubud, Bali, Indonesia, is dedicated to building with nature, incorporating sustainable materials and taking a climate-responsive approach. “Imagine a home that stays cool in summer without constant air conditioning, or warm in winter with minimal heating, simply by virtue of its design,” the studio says. “This isn’t magic; it’s the intelligent application of climate responsive architecture. In Sanskrit, “shala” means “home,” and the spiritual practice of yoga is complemented by purpose-built pavilion designs that encourage harmony and calm. Pablo Luna Studio’s Manta Shala is yet another example, perched on the coastline of Nusa Penida, Indonesia, with an undulating roofline that evokes the way a manta ray’s body creates a gentle, wave-like motion as it swims.

bodyOriginal.text: Sarcopenia is the name given to severe age-related loss of muscle mass and strength. This loss occurs steadily throughout later life. The present state of research into this condition is representative of aging more generally, in that while a range of quite different mechanisms all have strong supporting evidence for a meaningful contribution to sarcopenia, their relative importance to one another is unclear, how they connect to one another at the detail level is unclear, which are largely causes and which are largely consequences of one another, and their relationship to the known underlying forms of cell and tissue damage that drive aging is unclear. See the evidence for loss of muscle stem cell function to be the primary cause of sarcopenia, and surrounding discussions on that topic, for example. Here, researchers point instead to disruption of lactate metabolism in both liver and muscle tissue as the primary cause of sarcopenia; the involvement of the liver a reminder that no one tissue stands alone in the matter of aging. All organs communicate with one another and are interdependent in many different ways.

Sarcopenia is a progressive disease characterized by age-related decline in skeletal muscle force and mass. The fundamental molecular pathogenesis of sarcopenia has not yet been elucidated. Here, we show that the accumulation of lactate and intracellular acidification, lactic acidosis , in skeletal muscle owing to impaired liver-skeletal muscle lactate metabolism is the fundamental cause of sarcopenia. Systemic lactate tolerance decreased in aged mice owing to the impaired lactate processing capacity in the liver, which caused lactic acidosis in skeletal muscle.

Furthermore, pharmacological activation of hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF) or liver-specific activation of HIF1α improved age-associated impairment in lactate tolerance, lactic acidosis in skeletal muscle, and sarcopenia. Mechanistically, the decreased nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide level was the cause of dysregulated skeletal muscle functions due to lactic acidosis. Using mouse models , our results show lactic acidosis in skeletal muscle as a key molecular pathogenesis of sarcopenia and highlight HIF1α in the liver as a pharmacological target for sarcopenia.

bodyOriginal.text: Normal cell metabolism , particularly the activities of mitochondria , generates oxidizing molecules that react with proteins to disrupt their function. This damage occurs constantly, and is repaired constantly. Cells remove damaged proteins, undo oxidative changes, and make use of antioxidant enzymes such as SOD1 to prevent damage from occurring in the first place. With age, oxidation increases and becomes an important component of cell dysfunction. Here, researchers note that SOD1 itself can become oxidized and harmful, and discuss the importance of antioxidants disabled by oxidization in the growth of age-related oxidative stress in cells. The specific focus is on skin aging, but the points have relevance to all tissues.

As the body's primary barrier against environmental insults, the skin is continually exposed to oxidative stress, which may contribute to progressive proteotoxic stress. Excess reactive oxygen species (ROS) can overwhelm cellular protein-quality-control systems, promoting the accumulation of damaged and misfolded proteins, proteome instability, and eventual protein homeostasis ( proteostasis ) collapse. Superoxide dismutase 1 (SOD1) , a Cu/Zn-dependent cytosolic antioxidant enzyme and key component of cellular defense against superoxide radicals, is itself vulnerable to oxidative modification. ROS-mediated post-translational oxidation of SOD1 may promote its misfolding and the formation of toxic protein species, potentially establishing a self-amplifying cycle of superoxide accumulation, further protein damage, and impaired cellular homeostasis .

In cutaneous cell types, including dermal fibroblasts and epidermal cells, these processes may be especially relevant to age-associated declines in proteostatic capacity and skin aging. This review distinguishes established skin-specific evidence from hypotheses extrapolated from other systems and synthesizes current evidence on the interplay among ROS-induced protein damage, proteostasis failure, SOD1 dysfunction, and cutaneous aging. We highlight the bidirectional relationship between proteostasis collapse and mitochondrial dysfunction , which may establish a self-reinforcing cycle of oxidative stress, cellular senescence , and chronic low-grade inflammation . These interconnected processes may converge to promote extracellular-matrix remodeling and tissue dysfunction, contributing to wrinkles, reduced elasticity, and impaired barrier function.

bodyOriginal.text: Over 30 designers, makers and studios have created limited-edition and prototype furniture and objects for Lobby, a new design platform launched by recruitment agency Collate Form during London Design Festival .
Collate Lobby's debut exhibition takes the form of a fictional hotel suite and foyer, inspired by the fashion and interiors of the 1930s.

bodyOriginal.alt: Collate Lobby exhibition at London Design Festival

bodyOriginal.text: Over 30 designers and makers created furniture and objects for the collection Almost everything on show was developed by designers especially for Lobby, with standouts including a polished metal mirror by Jaclyn Pappalardo , a chainmail partition screen by Edward John Milton and a lounge chair by Matthew Coules .

The collection also includes small objects and accessories, including a lacquered resin lamp by Alexander Shayle , a cast bronze table lighter by Thomas Wheller , colourful silk scarves by Les Keepers and espresso cups by Maison S Sommet .

bodyOriginal.alt: Mirror by Jaclyn Pappalardo at Collate Lobby

bodyOriginal.text: Standouts include a polished metal mirror by Jaclyn Pappalardo Founder James Garis conceived Lobby as a platform for emerging and established designers to develop new product concepts and test them on the market.
It is intended to be a platform that sits somewhere between a brand and a retailer, giving designers freedom to experiment but maintaining a degree of curation.

bodyOriginal.alt: Maille by Edward John Milton at Collate Lobby

bodyOriginal.text: Edward John Milton contributed a chainmail partition screen, while Josh Page's Acid floor lamp features a base of carved teak-veneer plywood "I've met so many amazing, talented designers and makers over the years, but they have nowhere to funnel their work through in any sort of a controlled sense," Garis told Dezeen.
"There are services and websites that any decent designer can put their work on, but they aren't curated, so it never feels like a brand," he said.

bodyOriginal.alt: Vega Lounge Chair by Matthew Coules at Collate Lobby

bodyOriginal.text: The Vega lounge chair by Matthew Coules features alongside a textile work by Andrew Pierce Scott Lobby's model differs in that, for each product drop, participating designers and makers are asked to respond to a distinct theme.
For the inaugural drop, Garis asked for an object that deserves to live in a Parisian "boudoir-like" hotel. He then worked closely with participants on the final stages of product development.

Read: London has "the best architecture and interior design community in Europe" says Duncan Riches All objects are available to order, with Lobby holding exclusive rights for a minimum of three years.
Those that prove most successful will become part of Lobby's core collection.

bodyOriginal.alt: Bold Table by Odd Universe at Collate Lobby

bodyOriginal.text: Odd Universe's Bold table stands at the foot of a bed with linen by 2LG Studio "So many people in the industry get screwed over by brands, but we're trying to be as fair as possible," said Garis.

"I'm not a designer, but I am a furniture geek, and I understand what sells," he added. "[This model] gives me a chance to see what I can do for these designers, and if it doesn't work, then they can take the idea somewhere else."

bodyOriginal.alt: Works by Alexander Shale at Collate Lobby

bodyOriginal.text: Alexander Shayle's Alcove lamp and Bloom vase were shown on a console table by Thomas Veryard Lobby is presenting its debut exhibition at Yorkton Workshops , the home of design studio Pearson Lloyd . Spread across two rooms, it includes a reception area, a lounge space and a bedroom.
More than 40 objects are presented across these different areas, with key themes including art-deco style and material experimentation.

bodyOriginal.alt: Lighter by Thomas Wheller at Collate Lobby

bodyOriginal.text: Small objects include a cast bronze table lighter by Thomas Wheller One example of this is Josh Page 's Acid floor lamp, which combines a base of carved teak-veneer plywood and a poplin shade with a blue embroidered seam.
Others include Charlie Humble Thomas ' Fred lamps, which pair sculptural blown-glass shades with blocks of polished British marble, and Odd Universe 's tetris-like aluminium side tables.

bodyOriginal.alt: Light by Stephanie Sommet and Roti Akinyelu at Collate Lobby

bodyOriginal.text: Stephanie Sommet and Roti Akinyelu created a lamp that recalls cast-iron radiators Other notable pieces include a textile wall hanging by Andrew Pierce Scott , a pair of tassel pendulums by Christopher Kelly , oak stools with pewter inlays by Theodóra Alfreðsdóttir and textured ceramic sconces by Stine Keinicke .
Lobby is on show at Yorkton Workshops in Hackney from 12 to 20 September as part of London Design Festival . See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world.

articles.summaryOriginal: Craft has become cool, while industrial design has lost its sparkle. What's driving the trend? And are they really so different? Debika Ray reports. Just like the food industry before it, the world of design has internalised the language of The post How craft conquered design appeared first on Dezeen .

bodyOriginal.text: Craft has become cool, while industrial design has lost its sparkle. What's driving the trend? And are they really so different? Debika Ray reports.

'Handmade', 'heritage', 'bespoke' – most of us are used to reading these words by now. Just like the food industry before it, the world of design has internalised the language of craft – that of the 'local', 'artisanal' and 'authentic'.
At London Design Festival (LDF) this year, exhibitions of craft abound.

These range from Reviving Craft at Somerset House , a show of more than 60 artisans from China curated by Beijing-based media entrepreneur Yang Lan to "create a dialogue between traditional craftsmanship and contemporary design", to Wood for the Trees at the Tab Centre in Shoreditch , an "abstracted woodland" in which to contemplate responsible forestry, designed by London-based Mitre & Mondays for the American Hardwood Export Council .

bodyOriginal.alt: Symbiosis of Chrysanthemums II by Huang Lu

bodyOriginal.text: Among many craft-based exhibitions at this year's LDF is Reviving Craft, featuring pieces such as Symphony of Chrysanthemums II by Huang Lu. Photo courtesy of Reviving Craft From Milan to Copenhagen, it's the same story: where once objects on display were proudly modernist, minimalist, sleek and uniform, they are now just as likely to be textured and imperfect.
The growing status of collectible design is part of the same movement – the desire for unique objects met by the inherent unpredictability of the human hand.
Pavel Klimczak, founder of design retailer Monologue London , has noticed this desire in the questions his customers now ask him.

"People are becoming much more curious about the stories behind objects," he said. "They often come for the design, but quickly the conversation turns to them asking where a piece was made, who made it, how it was made, why it was designed that way and the material used."

Craft was once dowdy. Now it's cool. And industrial design – that 20th-century emblem of democratised mass production, functional innovation and accessible beauty – has, whether fairly or unfairly, somewhat lost its sheen.
What underlying social and economic tensions does this shift reveal? And, beyond face value, is the line between 'craft' and 'design' especially meaningful in the first place?

The growing interest in craft is often attributed to our modern condition: the frictionless and ephemeral nature of our daily interactions, the cold dead pieces of technology we're continuously pawing, the deceptive nature of digital content, and the stylistic uniformity imposed over decades by globalised mass production and online connectivity.
In that context, it's no surprise we're drawn to unique objects that carry traces of human intention, are made of materials we recognise and are connected to a time, person and place.

A greater interest in the local, in heritage and in the vernacular also tracks with the current political mood: the simultaneous return, globally, of traditional values and a growing focus on cultures that have long been marginalised by modernisation and globalisation.
London Craft Week founder Guy Salter is convinced that our renewed interest in craft is here to stay.

"It's not going anywhere soon, as it's built on solid foundations – on more than just fashionability," he said. "We're rediscovering [things about quality of workmanship] that our forefathers knew for hundreds of years."
"And whenever I travel, I meet people who aren't attracted by the glossiness of luxury brands, but instead feel pleased to be supporting craft on a community basis."

bodyOriginal.alt: Bamboo baskets with hand-blown glass made by Dima Srouji for a Gucci exhibition at Milan design week 2025

bodyOriginal.text: Gucci is among the brands to have incorporated craft into its presence at design festivals, as with these baskets made by Dima Srouji for an exhibition at Milan design week 2025. Photo by George Baggaley Drawing on this interest, London Craft Week (pictured top) now attracts about 250,000 visitors every year – up from about 35,000 a decade ago – which compares robustly to LDF's 475,000 in 2025.

This year, in a boost for its credentials, fashion designer Jonathan Anderson – who set up the €50,000 Loewe Craft Prize while creative director of the Spanish luxury house – came on board as a sponsor via his own brand, JW Anderson .
Alberto Merlo Carrero, Loewe Foundation's head of programmes, says the founding of the prize in 2016 was a recognition that contemporary craft was on the ascent.
"Extraordinary work was already happening around the world, yet the field remained relatively fragmented and often underrepresented within the broader cultural conversation," he said.
Fashion brands from Hermès to Gucci now more often than not tend to showcase craft in their increasingly visible presence at design weeks.
Fostering a healthy craft ecosystem requires long-term commitment, which – more broadly – hasn't always been evident.

Salter says the expansion and corporatisation of the luxury sector in recent years has shaken up a business model that a century ago was mostly based on "a small number of customers buying or commissioning from what were often family-owned luxury shops".

In the process of trying to attract a mass audience, he explains, money was channelled into marketing via flagship stores and advertising, with craft often taking a hit – the in-house artisan replaced by outsourced production, for example.
"Now, a number of brands have realised what was lost during that period, especially during the recent downturn, and are trying to retrofit it," he said.
Against that backdrop, Salter says, craft has become a marker of quality and trustworthiness.

He adds that, while initially those new "aspirational customers" they were after took brands at their word, today's buyers are more discerning, and trust companies with a track record of standing by their values.

bodyOriginal.alt: Peaches chair by Lara Bohinc

bodyOriginal.text: Lara Bohinc has worked in industrial design as well as making objects by hand, including the Peaches chair. Photo by Rebecca Reid In contrast, industrial design is facing a "difficult predicament" as people increasingly question the ethics and purpose of mass production, according to London-based designer Lara Bohinc , who has collaborated with brands for decades and recently started working with clay.
"We're drowning in products. There are too many brands, too many chairs, too many beds," she said.

Meanwhile, cheaper design is often associated with bad labour practices, unsustainable processes or toxic materials – factors that are often ignored because these products are what most people can afford.
Calling something craft and charging a lot for it doesn't necessarily change the ethics behind an object, though.

Between 2023 and 2026, luxury fashion brands including Armani, Dior and Valentino were placed under court monitoring in Italy after investigations found they had outsourced production to illegal workshops where undocumented migrants were working under exploitative conditions on supposedly artisanal products.
"Just because it's handmade doesn't mean it's angelic," Bohinc points out.
"Few are making money exclusively from selling objects they've made"

Andu Masebo , a London designer who creates functional objects and art pieces in wood and metal, says he never had a "romantic notion" around craft – rather, he started making his designs simply because of the difficulty of finding a company willing to produce them for him.
He points out that the rise of craft isn't only a story about what consumers want, but also of what the industry is producing.

For designers, for example, the move to making is often driven by a fragile job market in which brands favour existing names over investing in new work, leaving emerging designers with few options but to produce things themselves.

"I feel like there could be a more positive conversation around how we create conditions that allow people to work in design and not just in the gallery space, and a concerted effort by the industry to reach out to emerging talent, not just as a marketing tool but as a way of supporting the future design pool," he said.
While craft may be in vogue, Masebo has observed that making itself doesn't necessarily offer a more sustainable livelihood than working for a design company.
"Few of my peers are making money exclusively from selling objects and furniture they've made," he said.

bodyOriginal.alt: A4 lamp by Andu Masebo

bodyOriginal.text: Andu Masebo says he started making his own pieces, such as the A4 lamp, because of a lack of alternatives. Photo courtesy of Unit.d Instead, they use it to "express the highest version of their practice", while generating an income for themselves by diffusing that into a range of other related and unrelated sources, from social media to part-time jobs to commissions.

As Bohinc and Masebo highlight, categories such as craft and design may be useful from a marketing perspective, but underlying both are similar dynamics and challenges about quality, labour, employment and environmental impact that the sector cannot escape simply by changing how it describes work.
These extractive practices are among the subjects Nigerian-American designer Zoë Chinonso Ene is striving to address through her research and experiment-driven studio Homenkà .

In reality, she argues, craft and design aren't mutually exclusive categories, and the way we use those terms reveals underlying hierarchies in the value we place on different cultures of production – often based on aesthetic cues such as particular motifs, materials and styles.

"For example, with everyday objects from Igbo culture, I can see the decisions that were made to create object typologies for specific uses," said Ene, questioning why these are called craft rather than design.

Read: How London designers are making it work For LDF, Homenkà is creating an intervention as part of Brompton Design District – a parlour that will host evenings of play, eating, conversation and remembering "in the company of everyday design".
Its broader focus is on supporting craft ecosystems in Nigeria. In envisioning these, Ene isn't a purist about the separation between hand and machine.

"It may mean artisans working in a semi-industrialised space where they do 50 per cent, not 100 per cent, by hand, to speed it up while creating a fantastic product whose materials are sourced locally and gaining and exchanging skills," she said.
London designer Bethan Laura Wood has always straddled both worlds. She recalls that during her student days "craft was a dirty word in relation to design" – certainly not the case today.

For LDF, she is showing work as part of Craft x Tech , an exhibition by design studio Tangent that brings artisans from the Tōkai region of Japan together with international designers – in her case, to create folded hanging lamps made with shibori tie-dyeing company Suzusan .
Wood points out that public interest is like a pendulum – shifting from minimalism to maximalism, machine production to craft making – even as all these things continue to exist all at once.

bodyOriginal.alt: Nchọ by Homenkà, showing at LDF 2026

bodyOriginal.text: Zoë Chinonso Ene's designs drawing on Igbo culture at showing at this year's LDF. Photo by Christian Cassiel The reactionary resurgence of craft is also not a new thing – think of the Arts and Crafts movement emerging in response to the industrial revolution, she adds.
That's not to dismiss the significance of what's happening now: waves of fashion can leave behind more substantive and meaningful change.

"When industry started to pay more attention to recyclability or circular design , some companies just flirted with those ideas to tick boxes, but others adopted it into their systems in a long-term way," said Wood.
Similarly, beautifully produced videos revealing the process behind objects – the metal spinning, the turning pots, the scraping of lathes – probably won't dominate social media algorithms forever.

articles.titleOriginal: Are you getting ghosted more than ever? You're not alone!
articles.summaryOriginal: It's not about you; it's about a broken business culture. You've spent a lot of time, effort and emotional energy forging a working relationship. It's all going well. Then… nothing. The founder who sa...

bodyOriginal.text: It's not about you; it's about a broken business culture.

You've spent a lot of time, effort and emotional energy forging a working relationship. It's all going well. Then… nothing. The founder who said they loved your first concept simply vanishes. A marketing lead who's briefed you thoroughly and has promised a purchase order suddenly leaves you high and dry.

It's a horrible situation to be in. From a financial standpoint alone, it can be crippling. But more fundamentally, you also start to doubt yourself. Was the quote too high? Were the concepts lame? Did they find someone cheaper, or use AI? Did you have some food on your face during the Zoom call that everyone was too polite to point out?

Horrific, right? But here's what we've learned from our community on LinkedIn and Instagram . In 2026, ghosting has become systemic. So you shouldn't take it personally. Because it's not really about you at all.

Why silence has become the default "I've seen a lot of this so far this year, and it can feel really hollow at times," says director and cinematographer Rob Pinney . "I'm still getting a good number of approaches for new projects, but many more of those now end up with a dead email chain than before."

So what's behind the trend? "There seems to be a lot more budget hesitancy right now," Rob suggests. "And I suspect some of that is to do with clients weighing up that potential spend on video production, in my case, versus what they could do with it elsewhere, including with AI tools."

Film director Farai Dube has had similar experiences. "It's a lot of stop and start," he says. "When you're at the start of the conversation, there's actually a budget, but that's in jeopardy depending on sales and generally how much money's coming in. I get that: the part that's frustrating is keeping you on the hook. I'd rather have clarity upfront."

Yet it's not just cash-strapped clients who are guilty of ghosting. Creative director Rich Holt , for instance, complains about "recruiters who appeal for specific people to contact them—even though they're supposed to know the industry and have CVs on their desk already—and then just never reply." Director and lecturer Luke Tonge , meanwhile, calls out: "folks not replying when you invite them to speak at an event. It can hold up planning for weeks and even months."
So why does ghosting seem to be getting so much worse these days?

The fear factor Graphic designer and photo retoucher Sandrine Bascouert reckons there's something deeper going on than just laziness or poor organisation. "I think some people are afraid of communication as a whole," she says. "Ghosting has become a way to avoid normal conversations where there could be feelings hurt and disappointment."

That certainly chimes with my experience as a member of Generation X. When I first entered journalism in the 1990s, almost the entire job was phoning people. As long as you were polite and respectful, everyone was happy to chat.

By around the mid-2000s, though, I noticed that many creatives under 30 were screening their calls and wouldn't pick up if they didn't know the caller personally, even if they were actively trying to promote themselves and their work, which never made any sense to me.

Eventually I admitted defeat, and switched to email. But by the mid-2010s, many creatives were keeping their emails private—despite, again, ostensibly wanting self-promotion—and I had to start relying on social media DMs instead.

In 2026, many of those creatives are now seniors and CEOs. So it's no surprise to me that some might lack the ability to have difficult conversations, and not be willing to put in the emotional labour when times get difficult. I don't wish to generalise about an entire generation, of course. But still.

Good reason or bad actor? Poor communication skills, though, are only one reason for ghosting: there are plenty more. If we're being generous, for instance, we might assume that there's been something like a family emergency, and the other party just doesn't have the capacity to even open their inbox right now.

At the other end of the spectrum, some people can just be dicks. We've all heard of companies who interview people, ask for their ideas, and then simply steal them. There was never any job, freelance work or collaboration opportunity in the first place. It was all a scam.

Then there are those who sit somewhere in the middle, who aren't malicious, but just fail to cope. That doesn't help you , of course. As designer Nicholas Robb points out: "It starts to feel unfair after you've done a couple of calls with the stakeholders, bordering on consultation to help them scope it up. It would take 30 seconds to email back and say 'not interested + a reason why'."

Yet as an entrepreneur himself, he can also empathise. "I think business owners in particular are just so overwhelmed these days that they can't afford the time or mental space to do even that," he reflects. "So I try not to take it personally."
How we should respond Other than not beating yourself up for being ghosted, though, what can you practically do?

As a rule of thumb, designer Alexander Clark has developed a script. "After two or three of my emails go unreplied, I write this", he says, " Since I've not heard from you, I'll be pausing this and moving forward with other projects. Please let me know when you'd like to proceed or if you've changed priorities. " It usually yields a response within a day."

This is a good strategy because it removes all ambiguity. You've stopped chasing them (giving them the power) and are about to close the door (giving you the power). They have no choice but to make a decision. At this point, silence and doing nothing becomes a decision in itself.

And if that's what happens? Then move on, feeling empowered that you took control of the situation. And remember: their silence is not a poor reflection on you; it's a poor reflection on their lack of professionalism and communication skills.

Setting boundaries upfront Ultimately, prevention is always better than cure. So if you want to avoid getting ghosted, it's always good to set boundaries upfront, such as a deadline for responding to proposals. That might seem a little overbearing, but remember that clients and employers are often super-busy, and a deadline can actually be helpful for them too.

Content creator Jacob Elias Nurse offers a further suggestion: have a lot of plates spinning. "One thing I've learned from my nine months of being a full-time freelancer is that keeping busy helps you not worry too much about replies from companies that want to dangle a carrot in your face," he explains. "If you keep grinding at your craft, the money will follow."

He even finds a way to frame ghosting as a positive . As he puts it: "Their disrespect isn't a reflection of your craft or your quote. If anything, it helps you weed out who you want as a client and who you don't want as one."

Founder and creative director Kirsten Murray agrees. "A person who ghosts you is not someone you want to work with," she says. "Mutual respect and open communication make for the best creative partnerships."

So maybe that's the main takeaway. Ghosting sucks, for sure, but it's not necessarily a calamity. In fact, in the long term, it could be a good thing: saving you from a nightmare client and freeing you up to find a good'un instead.

articles.summaryOriginal: Researchers have established how a protein that is nearly absent in the literature, PTCHD4, is linked to cellular senescence. Very little previous work In most papers, after a customary discussion of […]

bodyOriginal.text: Researchers have established how a protein that is nearly absent in the literature, PTCHD4, is linked to cellular senescence .

Very little previous work In most papers, after a customary discussion of the mechanics of cellular senescence and current methods of handling it and its repercussions, the researchers go on to discuss previous work relating to the particular approach at hand. However, that does not pertain to this paper; PTCHD4 is only known as being structurally related to PTCH1, which affects the Hedgehog signaling pathway [1]. While some work has linked dysregulation of Hedgehog pathways to accelerated neurodegeneration [2], the specific role of PTCHD4 was not clear.

The researchers found that, when exposed to the genotoxin bleomycin, PTCHD4 increases alongside inflammation markers in a variety of cells, including human fetal lung diploid fibroblasts, mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs), alveolar epithelial type II cells (AEC2s), human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs) and adult retinal pigment epithelial cells. Aging Atlas data confirmed this upregulation in other types of cells as well, and NCBI data listed this molecule as being disease-associated: its presence is negligible under ordinary conditions.

The team then examined young mice, old mice, and progeric mice, staining for PTCHD4 alongside the senescence biomarker p16. The two biomarkers were expressed in similar quantities among each group in multiple tissues. Similar results were found in human tissue samples; idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) patients expressed more PTCHD4 in their lungs than people without the disease, and human lung cells expressing PTCHD4 were more likely to also express established senescence markers.

Significant effects on senescence The next experiment involved creating MEFs that do not express PTCHD4 and then driving them senescent through replication. PTCHD4 was found to be a critical driver of senescence in this group; after an average of eight passages, ordinary MEFs exhibited signs of senescence, such as the key biomarker SA-β-gal, while this did not occur to the PTCHD4-deficient MEFs until an average of passage 14.

This line of experimentation continued with PTCHD4-overexpressing MEFs, which began exhibiting senescence-related features such as SA-β-gal early in passage 5. Similar results were found in AEC2s; the inflammatory biomarkers IL6 and IL8, along with SA-β-gal, were upregulated alongside PTCHD4 overexpression.

This testing continued with live mice. The researchers utilized mice that do not express PTCHD4 along with wild-type mice, and they exposed both groups to D-galactose, which mimics many of the symptoms of natural aging. The mice that did not express PTCHD4 were much more resistant to D-galactose than wild-type mice, and there were no detectable physical or biochemical problems caused by this absence.

The team then continued with naturally aging animals. They found that mice that do not express PTCHD4 naturally live months longer than wild-type mice, and mice without it apparenly do not develop white hair the way that wild-type animals do.

bodyOriginal.alt: PTCHD4 aging

bodyOriginal.text: A further experiment involved subjecting mice to bleomycin, which harms lung function in a way that mimics IPF in people. As expected, the mice exhibited features of lung fibrosis within 21 days. However, the PTCHD4-less mice suffered from fewer symptoms of the disease, retaining more lung capacity, less immune infiltration, less destruction of alveolar tissues, and less fibrosis than wild-type mice.

A well-known signaling pathway In this study, PTCHD4 was found to have no effects on the Hedgehog pathway or related genes. Instead, its effects were found to be due to AKT signaling. AKT activation normally increases with aging, but a lack of PTCHD4 diminished this. The team created MEFs that do not express PTCHD4 but express AKT through a different construct, and these MEFs were not protected by their lack of PTCHD4. Similar experiments involving the direct expression of AKT in other cell types confirmed these results, recapitulating the effects of PTCHD4.

The researchers believe that “PTCHD4 may represent a candidate target for senescence-associated interventions” and that there is “a potential role for PTCHD4 in age-related fibrotic disease.” However, this is an initial study. Further work will need to be done to confirm these results, elucidate the relationship of PTCHD4 and AKT, ascertain any side effects of eliminating or suppressing PTCHD4, and determine if PTCHD4 can be targeted by interventions.

bodyOriginal.text: A few species of hydra are immortal in their normal environmental conditions, meaning that function does not decline over time and mortality risk does not increase over time. Researchers spent a good deal of time taking care of hundreds of hydra some years ago to demonstrate that this is the case . Hydra are lower animals, essentially a bundle of stem cells capable of regenerating and replacing any part of their bodies, somewhat analogous to an ambulatory embryo. It is an open question as to whether anything we can learn from their biochemistry can be useful in human medicine.

In today's open access paper, researchers report on the employment of telomerase by hydra. Telomeres are repeated sequences at the end of chromosomes that shorten with each cell replication , creating a clock that leads to cell death when telomeres are too short. In most species, somatic cells are limited in this way in order to minimize the risk of cancer, while stem cells employ telomerase to maintain long telomeres while delivering a supply of new daughter somatic cells to replace losses. The body is just a temporary vehicle for an immortal population of germline stem cells, in one view. Hydra are obvious very different in terms of the balance between stem cell behavior versus somatic cell behavior in individuals.
Telomerase expression and activity in the immortal cnidarian Hydra

Most living eumetazoan animals are mortal. A fundamental mechanism underlying cellular and organismal aging in many species is the progressive shortening of telomeres - protective nucleoprotein structures at chromosome ends. The finite replicative lifespan of somatic cells is linked to telomere attrition. The discovery of telomerase, a ribonucleoprotein complex with reverse transcriptase activity that synthesizes telomeric repeats, provided a molecular explanation for the unlimited proliferative potential of germlines, stem cells, and most cancer cells. In humans, telomerase is not expressed in most somatic tissues and is active primarily in germ cells, stem cells, and certain rapidly renewing tissues such as blood or intestinal epithelium .

Comparative studies indicate that telomere dynamics correlate with lifespan, with slower shortening rates in long-lived species. Recent cross-species analyses, however, reveal a more complex picture, suggesting that the relationship between telomere maintenance strategies (telomerase activity vs. alternative lengthening ) and longevity is not strictly deterministic. Nevertheless, it remains a prevailing hypothesis that biologically immortal organisms must possess robust mechanisms for telomere maintenance. Supporting this, sustained telomerase activity in somatic tissues has been documented in non-senescent invertebrate models such as planarians and long-lived bivalves .

Importantly, several taxa , including some hydras, planarians, and rotifers , have been reported to exhibit negligible or undetectable senescence. In this study, we characterized the telomerase of Hydra vulgaris . The expression pattern of the telomerase catalytic subunit (hyTERT) mRNA correlates with regions exhibiting high proliferative potential and remains unchanged during budding or regeneration. These findings were further corroborated by measurements of telomerase activity. Our data suggest that telomerase may play a role in the immortality of Hydra.

bodyOriginal.text: Tulu Health has launched in the US, betting that AI built for patient relationships can plug the churn draining membership clinics.

Dr Adil Khan didn’t set out to build a healthcare company in the US first. Tulu Health , the AI-driven platform he runs as CEO, started in India, then moved to the UAE, then Southeast Asia. Only now, after three prior markets, has it arrived in the country most people would assume comes first.

There’s a reason for the detour. India, Khan says, is a market “where healthcare complexity is measured not in millions of patients but in billions.” Fragmented systems. Payer landscapes that shift by region. Clinical teams working from decades of institutional habit rather than a shared playbook. If a platform could survive that, the thinking went, everywhere else would be easier by comparison.

What it learned along the way wasn’t really about India, the UAE, or Southeast Asia specifically. It was a pattern that kept repeating: longevity clinics and medspas were losing members they didn’t even know they were losing. Quietly. At scale. Every single day.
A number most clinics don’t track closely enough

Membership churn at longevity clinics and medspas runs 15% to 20% a year, according to Tulu Health [ 1 ]. That number doesn’t announce itself the way a bad marketing quarter does. It shows up slowly, in a member who came in twice and then stopped answering the phone, in a follow-up that never got scheduled. By the time a clinic notices, a good chunk of that revenue is gone, and replacing a lapsed member costs three to five times more than keeping the one already there.

Khan’s read on why this keeps happening is blunt: the software clinics already use wasn’t built for it. Legacy EHRs, generic CRMs bolted on after the fact, standalone booking apps – they each solve a piece of the problem, but none of them follow a member’s relationship with a practice from the first phone call through years of membership.

Tulu Health’s answer is built around what it calls a Patient Twin, essentially a continuously updated profile of each patient that four separate AI tools read from and write back to. AI Recall goes after patients who’ve gone quiet, reaching them in whichever language and channel they’re actually likely to respond to. AI Front Desk picks up every inbound call or message around the clock, so nothing lands in voicemail. AI Care Navigator tracks who’s supposed to be doing what, next follow-up, next test, next check-in, and flags the gaps. A fourth tool, AI Benchmarks, is still coming and will let a clinic see how it stacks up against comparable practices.
None of the four require a full rebuild. Clinics can plug in whichever one addresses their most expensive problem first, then add from there.
Why Khan keeps saying this isn’t about the software
Ask Khan what the hardest part of entering a new country is, and he doesn’t point to the technology.

“Entering a new healthcare market is not a product problem. It’s a trust problem,” he said. “You cannot deploy AI inside a clinic without people who understand the clinical, operational, and regulatory context of that specific market.”

That’s the reasoning behind bringing in Dr Sanjiv Chopra, Faculty Dean for Continuing Medical Education at Harvard Medical School, whose involvement in the company’s clinical governance predates the US launch and now extends board-certified oversight into it.
Tulu Health says it already runs inside more than 50 longevity clinics and medspas spread across three continents, a base it’s using as its evidence for the US pitch rather than a fresh promise.

There’s an easy version of this story where AI is the interesting part. It probably isn’t. Longevity medicine works on the premise that people keep showing up, for monitoring, for adjustments, for the slow accumulation of small interventions that only pay off over years. A member who quietly stops answering the phone isn’t just a line item disappearing from a clinic’s books; it’s someone who was supposed to be on a longevity plan and, for reasons a spreadsheet won’t catch, isn’t anymore.

“Every new market is a new chance to prove that the right AI, in the right hands, changes what’s possible for patients,” Khan said. Whether that holds will come down to something less flashy than the algorithm: whether clinics actually use it to keep the people they already signed up.

bodyOriginal.text: PhytoGaia spotlights new clinical data on ingredients for healthy aging, liver support and, notably, pet wellness.

Walk the floor of a nutraceutical trade show, and you’ll find plenty of companies promising the next big thing in healthy aging. What makes PhytoGaia ’s pitch at Vitafoods Asia 2026 worth a second look is where its ingredients start: palm fruit, run through a formulation strategy that spans human skin, human livers and, increasingly, pet coats.

The Malaysia-based supplier presented its lineup at the trade show, which ran 2–4 September at the Queen Sirikit National Convention Center in Bangkok, with three branded ingredient lines at the center of its pitch: STGaia, TocoGaia and PetGaia [ 1 ].

The headline ingredient is STGaia, a plant-based complex combining squalene and tocotrienols, a form of vitamin E found naturally in palm oil. PhytoGaia is positioning it as a “next-generation” ingredient for healthy aging, built around what it describes as an “outside-in” and “inside-out” strategy, meaning the same active compound is being explored both as a supplement people take and as an ingredient formulated into things applied to the skin. New clinical insights the company plans to share point to potential uses spanning longevity, beauty and general wellness.

It’s a strategy that reflects where the wider healthy-aging market has been heading: rather than treating supplements and skincare as separate categories, suppliers are increasingly designing single ingredients meant to work from both directions.

Alongside STGaia, the company presented new clinical evidence for TocoGaia, a full-spectrum complex of tocotrienols and tocopherols, the two natural forms that make up vitamin E. The research focuses on liver health, including potential applications for two conditions that have become a growing focus in metabolic health circles: metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease and alcohol-associated fatty liver disease.

Both are essentially forms of fat buildup in the liver, one linked to metabolic issues like obesity and diabetes, the other to alcohol use, and both are increasingly discussed as targets for the kind of early intervention that longevity-focused medicine tends to prioritize.

Perhaps the most unusual line in the showcase is PetGaia, a palm fruit extract PhytoGaia has developed specifically for companion animal skin and coat health. The company points to a randomized, placebo-controlled clinical study in dogs that found measurable improvements across several clinically assessed skin and coat parameters. It’s a small but telling sign of where the healthy-aging conversation is spreading: pet owners increasingly want the same kind of evidence-backed wellness products for their animals that they’re buying for themselves.

Beyond the raw ingredients, PhytoGaia demonstrated finished-product concepts built around them, including PetGaia softgels and dropper formats, STGaia vegetarian softgels, liquid capsules and functional jellies, alongside beauty-from-within concepts aimed at skin, hair and healthy aging more broadly.

“We provide branded, clinically researched phytonutrients with meaningful scientific and commercial value,” said Bryan See, Vice President of PhytoGaia, describing the company’s focus on helping brand owners, formulators and manufacturers turn ingredient research into products that actually reach shelves.

The company added that it is looking to deepen partnerships across the Asia-Pacific region, particularly in healthy aging and longevity, beauty-from-within, liver and metabolic health, and pet wellness.

What PhytoGaia’s showcase captures is a shift happening across the supplement industry more broadly: healthy aging is no longer a single-category pitch. The same underlying science, drawn here from a single crop, is being stretched across skin, liver and now animal wellness, a sign that ingredient suppliers see longevity less as one product category and more as a lens applied to everything they make.

bodyOriginal.text: New Princeton lab gives skincare-focused biotech direct control over research behind its flagship rapalog serum, rather than renting it out.

Most young biotechs outsource their early research, borrowing lab time, equipment and staff from wherever they can get it cheaply. Rapalogix Health just did the opposite. The Carlsbad, California-based company, which is building a business around a still-emerging category it calls longevity-based skin health, has announced that it has opened dedicated laboratory space at Princeton Innovation Center BioLabs in New Jersey, moving a chunk of its research in-house for the first time.

The facility, a life-sciences incubator operated by BioLabs and founded by Princeton University, gives Rapalogix access to fully equipped wet and dry lab space, shared scientific equipment, on-site technical staff and a surrounding community of life-science companies and academic researchers, all without the time and capital it would normally take to build that infrastructure from scratch. The lab became operational on 17 August 2026 [ 1 ].

Rapalogix’s research is built around rapalogs, a class of compounds tied to longevity signaling pathways in the body, applied specifically to skin biology rather than to the whole-body anti-aging space most people associate the term with. The company’s first commercial product, Re-Q Longevity Face Serum, is powered by a proprietary compound called RLX-201 and is already available through dermatology and aesthetic practices in the US.

From the new lab, the company’s research team plans to use 2D, 3D and more complex model systems to study how longevity pathways function specifically in skin tissue, map out the mechanisms behind its broader rapalog portfolio, test new formulations and generate the kind of proprietary data that future products will need to stand behind.

“Establishing our own laboratory is a deliberate step in how we build the evidence base for this category,” said Dr Rahul Mehta, CEO and co-founder of Rapalogix Health. “Generating data internally gives us direct control over the questions we pursue and the pace at which we pursue them, and it shortens the path from mechanistic insight to formulation. Princeton Innovation Center BioLabs gives us that capability alongside a community of scientists working on adjacent problems, and it lets us put capital into experiments rather than infrastructure.”
Longevity-based skincare is a young enough field that its own scientists talk about it as something still taking shape, not a settled discipline with established playbooks.

“There is so much to uncover as we pioneer longevity science, which represents a profound paradigm shift from the traditional approach to antiaging,” said Dr Manpreet Randhawa, executive director of research and development at Rapalogix Health. “Having immediate access to fully equipped wet labs and a forward-thinking scientific community allows us to move swiftly from hypothesis to validation, creating the rigorous science needed to genuinely push longevity and healthspan forward.”

That framing – longevity and healthspan rather than antiaging – is doing real work in how the company positions itself. Traditional anti-aging skincare has largely sold appearance: fewer wrinkles, firmer texture, a younger look. Rapalogix bets that the same longevity science being applied to organs and cellular pathways elsewhere in the body can be pointed at skin specifically, treating it as living tissue whose functional decline can be measured and slowed, not just cosmetically masked.

On its face, a company opening a research lab isn’t dramatic news, but for a firm operating in a category that doesn’t yet have agreed-upon standards for what “longevity skincare” even means scientifically, owning the lab where that evidence gets generated is a meaningful bet on credibility. It signals that Rapalogix intends to compete on data rather than marketing claims, in a segment of the beauty and wellness industry that has historically leaned hard on the latter. Whether RLX-201 and the rapalog class more broadly can deliver measurable, functional improvements in aging skin is the question this lab now exists to answer, on the company’s own terms and its own timeline.
