bodyOriginal.text: A Tohoku University team just won $1 million in a global healthspan prize for particles engineered to hunt down the cells that make us old.

Part of a ten-part series profiling each of the $101 million XPRIZE Healthspan competition’s Milestone 2 Awardees . Across the series, Longevity.Technology examines the science behind each team’s approach, the trial data supporting it and what stands between them and the competition’s final phase.

Keisuke Goda has spent years thinking about a strange design flaw in the human body: some of our cells refuse to die when they should. They just sit there, doing damage. Now his lab thinks it has found a way to send in a fix, and the judges of one of the largest health research competitions on the planet agree it is worth a serious look.

Goda, who leads a research team at the SiRIUS Institute of Medical Research and Graduate School of Medicine at Tohoku University , working alongside chemists at the University of Tokyo , has just been named a Milestone 2 Awardee of the XPRIZE Healthspan competition [ 1 ]. The team was chosen from a field of more than 600 entrants worldwide and collects a $1 million award to fund further testing.

To understand why that matters, it helps to know what the team is targeting: senescent cells. These are cells that have stopped dividing but, instead of clearing out of the body the way they are supposed to, stick around. Scientists have increasingly linked their buildup to the aches, slowdowns, and diseases that come with age. Think of them less as dead weight and more as cells stuck on an old shift, still clocked in long after they should have gone home, quietly wearing down everything around them.

Clearing them out has become one of longevity science’s most active pursuits. Goda’s lab has taken an unusual route: rather than killing senescent cells outright, his team built a delivery system to repair the tissue around them.
Aged mouse before and after the administration of Super Exosomes

The tool is something the researchers call a “super exosome.” Exosomes are naturally occurring particles that cells already use to ferry material to one another – nature’s own courier service. Goda’s team modified the surface of these particles with lanthanide ions, a chemistry tweak that dramatically sharpens their ability to home in on senescent cells specifically. Once attached, the particles unload their cargo: growth factors and genetic material aimed at repairing the surrounding tissue.

In mice, across multiple aged cohorts, the effect showed up in measurable ways: improved frailty scores, better physical performance, and gains across several other markers researchers use to track age-related decline, all without raising safety concerns. Using standard methods for translating results between species, the team estimates the benefit could correspond to more than 15 additional healthy years in humans. That is an early, mouse-derived projection, not a guarantee. The real test starts now.

To find out whether the projection holds, the team is moving into clinical studies with Tohoku University Hospital and the university’s Healthspan Research Center. The bar they need to clear for the XPRIZE Grand Prize is steep: proof that the therapy extends healthy human lifespan by at least ten years.

If the science holds up outside of mice, the lab believes the same delivery platform could reach well beyond frailty – into cognitive and immune function, hair regeneration, skin rejuvenation and reproductive medicine. Commercialization plans are already taking shape through a venture called NanoTitan, which would handle manufacturing and distribution of any resulting therapies out of Japan.
Goda frames the milestone as a step, not a finish line.

“Advancing to the XPRIZE Healthspan finals is an important milestone, but our ultimate goal is to translate this technology into therapies that allow people to lead healthy, independent, and active lives longer,” he told Asia Research News . “We look forward to validating this approach in human clinical studies and bringing its benefits to society.”

What makes this story worth watching isn’t just the prize money; it’s what the approach represents. Much of longevity research has chased ways to kill off senescent cells outright. Goda’s team is testing a different bet: leave the damaged cells be, but flood the surrounding tissue with the raw materials to repair itself. If that logic holds up in people the way it did in mice, it could open a second front in how the field tackles aging tissue, one aimed less at demolition and more at repair.

A little over a year ago, HexemBio was a single-idea company: take a patient’s own aging blood stem cells, briefly place them back in a lab-built version of the environment where the body first made them […] The post HexemBio raises $15.5m to rejuvenate aging ste

bodyOriginal.text: Berkeley biotech’s stem cell rejuvenation platform, built for transplant medicine, is branching into an injectable and a skin treatment.

A little over a year ago, HexemBio was a single-idea company: take a patient’s own aging blood stem cells, briefly place them back in a lab-built version of the environment where the body first made them before birth, and return them rejuvenated. That idea is still the core of the business. However, the San Francisco-based company announced today that it has built two additional products on top of it, backed by $15.5 million in total funding, with new investor Happiness Capital joining existing backers Draper Associates and Boost VC.

HexemBio’s technology is called the Synthetic Human Yolk Sac , a lab-recreated version of the developmental environment where a person’s first blood-forming stem cells arise before birth. The company’s approach takes a patient’s own aged stem cells, exposes them briefly to that environment outside the body, then reinfuses them, aiming to restore some of the regenerative capacity those cells had earlier in life. The platform has been published in Nature , with additional manuscripts under review, and the company has filed 17 patent applications worldwide, two of which have been granted so far.

The first-generation program built on that technology is a cell therapy aimed at improving outcomes in bone marrow transplants for patients with blood disease, a procedure that remains grueling and, for a meaningful share of patients, doesn’t fully restore normal blood cell production afterward. HexemBio received Orphan Drug Designation for the program in July 2025, completed its pre-IND meeting with the FDA in January 2026, and is targeting first-in-human trials in 2027.

This week’s news centers on that first program. A second-generation product is an injectable designed to carry the same developmental signals as the yolk sac environment, without requiring a patient’s cells to be collected and processed outside the body first. It’s aimed at people who could benefit from restored stem cell function but who fall outside the transplant setting altogether, and it’s currently in advanced preclinical development. A third-generation product, aimed at enhancing and protecting skin, is in the final phase of development, with what the company describes as an aggressive go-to-market plan.

“Our first generation product and lead program for transplants is still the main priority to get into human clinical trials for 2027,” said Gabriel Levesque Tremblay, CEO and co-founder of HexemBio. “Our goal is to create accessible therapies that extend healthy years.”

Eric Ng, CEO of Happiness Capital, framed the funding round around a broader mission: “We are excited by HexemBio’s approach to targeting the foundational drivers of aging, which will help people extend their healthspan and deliver benefits that resonate across generations.”

Draper Associates, the round’s lead investor, has a track record of backing science that sounds more speculative than it turns out to be, with recent bets on artificial wombs and de-extinction alongside earlier stakes in Tesla, SpaceX, Coinbase, Robinhood and Colossal.

“We invested in HexemBio’s first therapy, and we are thrilled with their progress,” said Tim Draper, founding partner at Draper Associates. “The team has been outstanding. Their fundamental breakthrough technology has expanded into three new product categories, maybe more to come.”
Blood stem cells as a longevity chokepoint

The transplant application is the most immediately practical of the three, but it’s worth sitting with why a synthetic developmental environment for blood stem cells matters beyond that one procedure. Hematopoietic stem cells, the ones that give rise to every type of blood and immune cell in the body, decline in both number and quality as people age, a shift that’s been linked to weaker immune responses, higher rates of blood disorders, and slower recovery from illness generally.

A platform that can coax those cells back toward a more youthful state, even briefly and even outside the body, is targeting one of the more upstream mechanisms in the aging process rather than treating downstream symptoms of it. HexemBio’s transplant program will be the first real test of whether that idea holds up in a person rather than a dish. If it does, the injectable and skin programs stop looking like separate side bets and start looking like the same underlying discovery, applied to more of the body.

articles.titleOriginal: Asymptomatic Persistent Infection as a Contribution to Degenerative Aging
articles.summaryOriginal: Persistent infections such as cytomegalovirus and other herpesviruses most likely accelerate aging, primarily via harmful effects on the immune system that lead to earlier immunosenescence and chronic inflammation than would otherwise be the case. A range of mechanistic and epidemiological research broadly supports this hypothesis. It remains challenging to completely clear persistent viral infect

bodyOriginal.text: Persistent infections such as cytomegalovirus and other herpesviruses most likely accelerate aging, primarily via harmful effects on the immune system that lead to earlier immunosenescence and chronic inflammation than would otherwise be the case. A range of mechanistic and epidemiological research broadly supports this hypothesis. It remains challenging to completely clear persistent viral infections, however. If a strong antiviral therapy existed , epidemiological data would likely prove the point one way or another within five to ten years, as effects on aging would become apparent in older populations. As it stands, the present relatively weak antiviral therapies show some evidence for positive effects on late life risk of mortality and age-related disease, but not in all studies.

Asymptomatic infections are traditionally considered harmless, reflecting effective immune control and the absence of clinical disease. Yet growing evidence shows that these silent encounters with microbes are far from being immunologically neutral. Throughout life, humans are challenged by a remarkably broad spectrum of viruses and bacteria, including latent pathogens that persist, fluctuate, or periodically reactivate without producing significant symptoms. From an evolutionary standpoint, this represents a fundamental trade-off. Long-lived hosts benefit from maintaining diverse commensal , latent, and low-grade persistent microbes that enhance immune readiness, promote cross-protective immunity , and reduce vulnerability to severe infections. However, this adaptive advantage is counterbalanced by the continuous burden of chronic, almost undetectable immune activation and inflammation, and by the energetic cost of sustaining such mechanisms of surveillance.

In this regard, retroviral integrations provide a striking illustration of how persistent viral presence has shaped the evolution of complex organisms by introducing new regulatory elements , immune modulators, and developmental programs. These ancient viral imprints demonstrate that clinically-silent host-microbe interactions can exert long-term selective pressures and influence species-specific biological trajectories. At the individual level, repeated asymptomatic infections trigger transient waves of immune activation, endothelial perturbation, mitochondrial stress, and complement engagement. Although each episode is mild and self-limited, their cumulative burden generates micro-damage that accelerates immunosenescence, perturbs metabolic and vascular homeostasis , and contributes to the progressive rise in systemic inflammation characteristic of aging.

articles.summaryOriginal: Cells become senescent constantly throughout life in response to various forms of damage and stress, ceasing replication and generating a potent mix of inflammatory signals. In youth, these cells are promptly cleared by the immune system, but with advancing age they begin to linger and accumulate. The inflammatory signaling becomes disruptive to tissue structure and function when sustained over th

bodyOriginal.text: Cells become senescent constantly throughout life in response to various forms of damage and stress, ceasing replication and generating a potent mix of inflammatory signals. In youth, these cells are promptly cleared by the immune system , but with advancing age they begin to linger and accumulate. The inflammatory signaling becomes disruptive to tissue structure and function when sustained over the long term, and this is an important contribution to degenerative aging. Here, researchers show that macrophage cells in the kidney express increasing amounts of the P2RX7 receptor on the cell surface as they progress towards becoming senescent, and blocking this receptor with a suitable antagonist small molecule reduces macrophage senescence and improves kidney function.

Macrophage senescence is a pathological feature in aging or diseased kidneys. However, the role of senescent macrophages in kidney injury and aging has not been fully elucidated yet. We integrated the analysis of single-cell RNA sequencing datasets and the adoptively transfusion of pretreated bone marrow-derived macrophages to investigate the role of renal macrophage senescence in kidney injury. Here, we portrayed the senescence trajectory along multiple time points in infiltrating macrophages, and observed the persistent increase of macrophage-expressed purinergic receptor P2RX7 along the senescence trajectory in injured kidneys of septic mice.

Importantly, our discovered small-molecule P2RX7 antagonist strikingly improved kidney function and pathological damage, as well as mitigated macrophage senescence in septic and aging mice. Mechanistically, P2RX7 antagonist could promote the wound healing , migration , and proliferation capacity of senescent reparative macrophages, thus exerting anti-inflammatory effects and repairing kidney tissues. Together, our findings illustrate the crucial participation of senescent macrophages in septic kidney injury, and offer novel therapeutic strategy via intervening P2RX7 against immunosenescence -associated kidney injury and aging.
Link: https://doi.org/10.7150/ijbs.138299

articles.titleOriginal: What this elegant redesign of a sparkling water brand teaches us about packaging in 2026
articles.summaryOriginal: Antwerp studio WeWantMore's refresh of BRU trades a second-long shelf glance for a seat at the table. It's become such a cliché in packaging design, you'd think it was law. Everything needs to be opti...

bodyOriginal.text: Antwerp studio WeWantMore's refresh of BRU trades a second-long shelf glance for a seat at the table.

It's become such a cliché in packaging design, you'd think it was law. Everything needs to be optimised for that single second a shopper glances at it on a shelf. It needs to stand out from the crowd, lure people in. You only have the time it takes for a heart to beat, so don't waste it. Throw everything you have into drawing the eye.

All of which makes a lot of sense. But it's useful to remember that not every single product is fighting for attention from tired and time-poor supermarket shoppers. Sometimes, packaging needs to do very different things.

Sparkling water is a great example. Many of us go to the supermarket for the low-cost stuff, where we expect them to pile it high and sell it cheap. But when we're in a restaurant, the design of a bottle—whether it's wine or water—is an important part of the experience.
In short, we want something to visually elevate our evening out. And that's something Belgian sparkling water brand BRU, which has long been associated with fine dining, understood well.

Who is BRU? BRU can trace its origins back to the 17th century, when it started bottling the natural spring water of Stoumont, in the Ardennes. In modern times, it's been commercialised as a table water brand through the Spadel group, with a name shortened from the French word bruisser (meaning to rustle or murmur).

bodyOriginal.alt: Three framed vintage-style BRU sparkling water posters and advertisements displayed on a wood-panelled wall above a formally set dining table with white tablecloths and glassware
Blue awning above a restaurant entrance featuring BRU branding and "Some things just belong on the table" tagline, with elegant wooden doors and stone facade behind

bodyOriginal.text: What is stylish and sophisticated at one time, though, can be perceived as old-hat and boring a few decades on. And in recent years, however, BRU had become increasingly perceived in this way.

WeWantMore , a creative agency founded in Antwerp in 2006, set out to change that, repositioning it "from a restaurant staple to the finishing touch for the table, designed for every meaningful moment shared around food." An important aspect of that was shifting the focus of the packaging from trying to stand out in the shop to being something people would be proud to display on their table.

Calm and disciplined The new packaging does a great job of putting that idea into practice. The tone is calmer, with a colour palette centred around a deep navy blue that both feels refined and evokes obvious associations with water.

bodyOriginal.alt: Clear glass bottle of BRU sparkling water with blue label featuring a deer motif and blue screw cap, casting a soft shadow against a cream background
Bottle of BRU sparkling water with a redesigned label featuring a blue leaping stag and bold typography against a white background
Three bottles of BRU sparkling water with white labels featuring a navy deer logo and typography, displayed against a neutral background

bodyOriginal.text: The existing brand emblem of a leaping stag is now sleek and sculptural, while avoiding the "minimise everything down to nothing" trend that might have robbed it of all its distinctiveness. And while the lettering is colourful and decorative, it never overwhelms the label, thanks to a disciplined approach to the use of white space.

The result is a design that delivers exactly what WeWantMore set out to achieve. A bottle that people would actively want in front of them while eating, and a brand slogan, "Some things just belong on the table", to drive it all home.

Key takeaways For designers in general, I'd say there are a couple of key takeaways from this story. Firstly, don't ever assume what your design needs to do. It might seem obvious to you that something, for example, needs to stand out on the shelves, but maybe it doesn't. Maybe it won't even appear on the shelves at all.

bodyOriginal.alt: La Touche Perlée logo in white typography on a deep blue background
Bright blue sculptural stag with branching antlers in a leaping pose against a cream background
Person holding a BRU sparkling water brand card displaying the logo and tagline "Naturally sparkling, some things just belong on the table

bodyOriginal.text: Yes, we all want to dive into making cool things as soon as possible. But before you open that Photoshop document, before you start brainstorming even, you need to be absolutely sure you understand the product, the business behind it, the target audience.

The second lesson, I think, is that heritage is an asset to treasure, but rarely needs to be preserved in aspic. WeWantMore could have kept its stag exactly as it was, or completely ditched it; both approaches would probably have been disastrous.

Instead, they subtly modernised it in a way that didn't alienate fans, but would also attract new ones. That's never an easy task, but if you pull it off as a designer, the world will soon be beating a path to your door.

articles.summaryOriginal: Despite considerable and growing effort put towards the development of novel means to slow and reverse aging over the past thirty years, the longest lived laboratory mice remain those lineages first established in the 1990s with mutations that disable growth hormone metabolism, such as via knockout of growth hormone or growth hormone receptor genes. These mice are small and vulnerable to cold, but

bodyOriginal.text: Despite considerable and growing effort put towards the development of novel means to slow and reverse aging over the past thirty years, the longest lived laboratory mice remain those lineages first established in the 1990s with mutations that disable growth hormone metabolism , such as via knockout of growth hormone or growth hormone receptor genes. These mice are small and vulnerable to cold, but live as much as 70% longer than their unmodified peers.

It seems likely that this has little relevance to human aging, as Laron syndrome is the analogous human inherited condition, usually caused by a growth hormone receptor loss of function mutation . Laron syndrome patients may have a lower incidence of some age-related conditions, but do not appear to live meaningfully longer than the rest of the human population. One of the most important lessons of the past thirty years of study of calorie restriction and growth hormone metabolism in the context of aging is that these interventions produce much larger effects in short-lived species than in long-lived species.

Nonetheless, disruption of growth hormone metabolism remains an active area of study. You might recall a paper published five years ago or so in which researchers showed that disruption of growth hormone metabolism starting in adult life , at six months of age in mice, still produced a slowing of aging. Here, the same team repeats the same effort starting at twelve months of age, mid-life for mice. The size of effect on life span is much the same in male mice when starting at this later age, but worse in female mice. In either case, the extension of life span is modest in comparison to life-long disruption of growth hormone metabolism, less than 10%. Like the existence of Laron syndrome, this argues against putting meaningful effort into attempts to build human therapies based on this mechanism.
Midlife Growth Hormone Receptor Ablation Extends Healthy Lifespan and Induces Sex-Specific Hepatic Transcriptional Changes at Single-Cell Resolution

Suppression of growth hormone (GH) signaling is known to be effective to extend lifespan in mammals, yet most models rely on congenital disruption of the GH/ insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1) axis. Whether modulation of this pathway later in life can still influence aging and the underlying cellular mechanisms remains incompletely understood. To address this, we ablated the growth hormone receptor (Ghr) at 12-months of age in mice (12mGHRKO), using a tamoxifen-inducible model.

This midlife Ghr disruption produced the expected endocrine signature of GH resistance, including reduced circulating IGF-1 and elevated GH levels. Importantly, lifespan was significantly extended in both sexes without major effects on somatic growth. Despite increased adiposity , male 12mGHRKO mice exhibited improved insulin sensitivity and protection against age-related deterioration of neuromuscular performance and bone microarchitecture . Single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) of liver tissue identified a reduction of B-cells in both sexes and a dimorphic transcriptional remodeling, including a shift toward feminized gene expression in male hepatocytes , marked by reduced male-biased gene expression and increased female-biased transcriptional programs, consistent with impaired pulsatile GH- STAT5 signaling.

Together, these findings demonstrate that suppression of GH signaling initiated in middle age is sufficient to reshape hepatic transcriptional programs and promote healthy longevity, supporting the GH/IGF-1 axis as a promising target for gerotherapeutic interventions.

bodyOriginal.text: Core Biogenesis and Faravelli are testing whether the biotech behind facial skincare can be scaled up to treat the rest of the body.

There’s a jar sitting on a lab bench in Strasbourg that isn’t for sale. That’s kind of the point. Core Biogenesis built it, alongside its Italian distribution partner Faravelli , purely to make an argument: that the same biotech doing serious work on faces could do just as much for the rest of the body, if anyone bothered to formulate it that way.
They’re calling it Skin Longevity Butter.

The gap it’s pointing at is a real one. Facial skincare has spent the past several years absorbing genuinely advanced science, lab-grown growth factors, barrier-repair peptides, actives with actual clinical trials behind them. Body care mostly hasn’t kept pace. A body butter is still, for most people, a body butter: something that moisturizes and smells nice. Core Biogenesis wanted to know what happens if you stop treating that as a given.

Two ingredients do the heavy lifting: Peauforia and Peauvita, proprietary biomimetic growth factor technologies Core Biogenesis developed using its own plant-based production platform [ 1 ]. In plain terms, they’re lab-made compounds engineered to behave like the growth factors skin already produces to repair itself, encapsulated in tiny lipid capsules called oleosomes that help carry the actives where they need to go. None of that would matter much if the formulation didn’t also feel like something people would actually want to use, so the team paired those actives with Illipe butter and a supporting lipid blend, aiming for a texture rich enough that the science doesn’t announce itself.
Tony Abboud, Chief Commercial Officer at Core Biogenesis, frames the logic simply.

“As skincare routines extend beyond the face, biotechnology offers an opportunity to create body care that supports skin quality, resilience and longevity,” he said. “Skin Longevity Butter provides a glimpse into what that future could look like.”

Skin Longevity Butter isn’t a one-off. It’s part of a wider Longevity Concepts collection the two companies have built together, which also includes a Lip Longevity Gloss and an Eye Longevity Shadow, both running the same growth-factor approach into color cosmetics rather than skincare proper. Taken together, the collection reads less like a product launch and more like a pitch deck aimed at other brands: here’s what’s possible if you’re willing to formulate around it.

That pitch lands at a moment when longevity has become one of beauty’s most reliable growth stories, no longer confined to the premium skincare shelf and increasingly showing up in hair care, body care, and now makeup. Ingredient suppliers have noticed, and they’re building the technology platforms to match.

None of it gets to a shelf, though, without a middleman most shoppers never think about. Faravelli distributes ingredients and helps brands turn a formulation concept into something a factory can actually produce at scale, work that sits well outside where most of the credit in a beauty launch usually lands. Deals like this one hint at distributors doing more of that translation work themselves rather than waiting for a brand to ask.

Whether Skin Longevity Butter itself ever shows up on a shelf is almost beside the point. The concept behind it, using biotechnology to get skin to repair and renew rather than simply sit under a layer of moisture, is where the industry’s longevity story seems to be heading next: fewer products built to hide what aging looks like, more built to interrupt it at the source. If body care follows the path facial skincare already took, the ingredient panel on a body butter may soon read a lot more like the one on a serum.

bodyOriginal.text: A new industry analysis maps 30-plus microbiome startups against longevity, and finds a field still torn between wellness and medicine.

For a long time, the gut microbiome sat in the “probably relevant, hard to prove” bucket of aging science. That changed, officially at least, in 2023, when the widely cited framework describing the hallmarks of aging, the biological processes researchers broadly agree drive us toward decline, expanded from nine categories to twelve. Gut dysbiosis, the breakdown of a healthy microbial balance in the digestive tract, made the cut. It’s now considered a driver of aging in its own right, not just a symptom of it.

A new landscape analysis from Plug and Play Ventures , a firm that scouts startups across health and biotech, takes stock of what’s actually being built in response. The team mapped more than 30 companies working at the intersection of microbiome science and longevity [ 1 ]. What comes back is a field with real scientific momentum and, frankly, a still-unresolved identity crisis.

Some of the underlying biology explains why investors keep circling back here. About 70% of the human immune system lives in the gut. Roughly 90% of the body’s serotonin, the neurotransmitter tied to mood, gets produced there too, not in the brain as most people assume. And unlike a person’s genome, the microbiome is something people can actually change through diet, lifestyle and now, increasingly, through targeted intervention.

The market has followed the science, more or less. According to the Microbiome Global Market Report 2026 , the global microbiome market grew from $295 million in 2020 to more than $800 million in 2025, and it’s projected to top $3 billion by 2035. Diagnostics, the tests that tell you what’s going on in your gut, still make up more than 80% of that market today. But therapeutics and active microbiome modulation, the products that try to actually change what’s happening rather than just report on it, are the fastest-growing slice. The field, in other words, is moving from measuring the problem to treating it.

The report organizes the startup landscape around four biological “levers,” though the lines between them blur more than any tidy framework suggests. Inflammaging, the chronic low-grade inflammation that builds quietly over decades, is the best understood of the four, tied to a weakened gut barrier that lets bacterial fragments leak into the bloodstream and trigger a slow-burning immune response linked to heart disease and type 2 diabetes. Metabolic health is the best-funded corner by a wide margin. Companies like Viome and Pendulum have raised hundreds of millions of dollars around the idea that gut bacteria shape how the body handles blood sugar and energy, a story that’s picked up extra relevance now that GLP-1 drugs dominate the metabolic conversation.

The gut-brain axis might be the most surprising piece of all this. Research published in Nature in 2024 found distinct microbiome signatures showing up years before the clinical symptoms of cognitive decline appeared, which raises the odd possibility that the gut functions as an early warning system for conditions like Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s. Then there’s the gut-skin axis, probably the least expected connection on the list, linking intestinal inflammation to visible aging: everything from eczema to accelerated collagen breakdown. It’s part of why L’Oréal, Unilever, and Estée Lauder have all quietly built out microbiome research programs of their own.

Worth remembering here: this isn’t the field’s first attempt. Kaleido Biosciences shut down in 2022. Evelo Biosciences closed in 2023. Seres Therapeutics, despite winning FDA approval for its therapy Vowst, ended up selling it to Nestlé Health Science in 2024 rather than commercialize it alone. The common thread, according to the report, is that these companies treated the microbiome as a single, isolated drug target, when it actually behaves as an interconnected system touching inflammation, metabolism, brain function and skin, more or less all at once. Newer entrants, armed with better sequencing and AI-driven modeling, are betting they can finally treat it that way instead.

One company the report singles out is Jona, a New York-based platform founded by Leo Grady, who previously led the AI pathology company Paige.ai to its first-ever FDA approval for an AI diagnostic product. Jona’s real difference isn’t the testing itself, but what happens after. Its AI cross-references a person’s results, which can flag more than 21,000 different microorganisms, against roughly 220,000 peer-reviewed studies, then simulates how different diets or supplements might shift that person’s biology before recommending anything.
“We’re seeing a real inflection point in consumer interest around the microbiome,” Grady said, noting that nearly half of Americans now report taking probiotics daily or almost daily [ 2 ].

Still, the report is candid that most startups in this space haven’t fully committed to a longevity positioning yet, leaning instead on general wellness claims or narrow disease indications. That’s starting to shift. Whether it shifts fast enough, and whether these companies end up getting judged by clinical trial data instead of gut-health marketing copy, is probably the question that decides which ones are still around in five years.

bodyOriginal.text: NGL 2026 will bring clinicians, scientists, founders and investors together to turn healthspan ideas into clinical action.

Next Generation Longevity 2026 will convene in Osaka, Japan, on 15–16 October, bringing together an international group of clinicians, researchers, founders, technologists and investors to examine how longevity medicine can move from a rapidly expanding body of knowledge into clinical and commercial practice. The inaugural two-day meeting will take place at Nakanoshima Qross, Osaka’s government-backed regenerative medicine innovation hub, with a program spanning precision medicine, biomarkers, applied AI, regenerative therapeutics and the business of healthspan.

Co-chaired by physicians Anant Vinjamoori and Deepti Agarwal, alongside Japan-based healthcare executive Naoko Kita, NGL 2026 has been deliberately designed as a relatively small, curated gathering rather than a conventional sequence of lectures and exhibition booths. Debates, fireside conversations, workshops and case-based Boardrooms will put different disciplines around the same problems – with implementation, rather than information alone, as the intended endpoint. The organizers’ own ambition for the gathering is not a modest one: they describe it as something like the World Economic Forum for longevity and the future of medicine – a global, cross-disciplinary room where debates and working Boardroom sessions take on some of the field’s most pressing open questions, in the hope that what surfaces there changes how the field actually operates, rather than simply how it talks about itself.

Longevity.Technology: Longevity science is hardly suffering from a shortage of information; the harder problem is what happens when that information leaves the paper or podium and encounters patients, clinical practice and economics. Translation increasingly demands different priorities in the same room – scientists asking what the evidence supports, clinicians what can responsibly be done and founders, investors and policymakers what can actually be built and scaled. Consensus may be comfortable, but structured disagreement is often more useful; NGL’s Boardroom format is interesting precisely because it is designed to pressure-test assumptions rather than manufacture agreement. Longevity medicine now sits at the collision point between frontier science and ordinary life, where biomarkers must inform decisions, AI must improve rather than decorate practice and regenerative medicine must make the difficult journey from possibility to application. Conferences are rather good at producing conversations – and business cards; the more meaningful measure is what survives the flight home. NGL’s emphasis on prototypes, partnerships and plans speaks to what the sector increasingly needs: not simply more knowledge about extending healthspan, but better ways of putting the useful parts to work.

The idea took shape on a trip to Japan. Co-chair Dr Anant Vinjamoori visited a year ago to give a talk and came away struck less by the country’s stem-cell science and regenerative medicine frameworks than by something harder to put on a slide: a culture in which longevity is simply how people live, day to day, rather than a frontier being pioneered. That distinction, worked through with the other co-chairs Dr Deepti Agarwal and Naoko Kita, became the seed of NGL – the conviction that the setting itself should be part of the argument, not just its backdrop.

The format also developed in response to the organizers’ experience of attending longevity conferences themselves. They saw value in bringing a young and unusually multidisciplinary field together, but felt that successive keynotes and conventional panels could leave participants with plenty to think about and rather less to do. Their response is a meeting intended to make the room itself part of the program – small enough for participants to contribute rather than simply observe, with connections curated around what individuals are trying to achieve.

Central to that approach is the NGL Boardroom, a business-school-style case format in which physicians, scientists, entrepreneurs, policymakers and investors work through unresolved decisions in longevity medicine. Clinical evidence may pull in one direction while technological feasibility, economics or regulation pulls in another; consensus is explicitly not required.
A core faculty will return across multiple sessions rather than appearing for a single presentation, allowing arguments to develop over the two days.

Anthony Molina (co-lead, Central Laboratory and Biorepository for XPRIZE Healthspan)
Raghav Sehgal (Forbes 30 Under 30 honoree and Faculty Member at Yale University)

Japan is more than a convenient pin on the conference map. Its population longevity and aging demographics make it an important real-world case study for healthspan medicine, while its regenerative medicine ecosystem offers a different perspective on how emerging therapies can progress toward clinical use. The organizers see the country as a potential bridge between international longevity medicine and a developing Asia-Pacific ecosystem.

The venue makes that argument rather literally. Nakanoshima Qross brings clinical care, R&D and an international forum together on one site; the conference will therefore discuss translational medicine within an infrastructure designed around translation rather than in the more familiar habitat of a hotel ballroom.

There is a cultural dimension too. The program sets regenerative therapeutics, precision diagnostics and AI alongside Japanese approaches to food, purpose and social connection. Accompanying experiences include matcha and fermentation traditions, with an optional post-conference study tour to Nagano complete with traditional Buddhist cuisine, shrine visit, a meeting with the town’s famous ‘Green Centenarians’ and a chance to enjoy the spectacular autumn foliage. The intention is not to confuse tradition with clinical evidence, but to consider healthspan as something lived as well as prescribed – a useful distinction when preventive medicine ultimately depends on what happens beyond the clinic.

The agenda begins with the biology and measurement of aging before moving deliberately toward application. Biomarker sessions will examine what current tools actually measure and where their clinical utility begins to fray; system-focused discussions will consider aging across the brain, heart, gut and endocrine system rather than treating biological age as one conveniently obedient number.

AI receives similar scrutiny. Alongside discussion of tools already scaling in clinical settings, a boardroom session will explore clinical workflow support, patient education and longitudinal personalized care. Regenerative medicine sessions will consider cellular therapies and Japan’s regulatory landscape, while another strand tackles insurance, policy and employer models – the less glamorous machinery through which preventive medicine either becomes part of healthcare or remains an attractive parallel universe.

That question of application extends to biological age testing itself. A dedicated discussion will look at how such testing is actually being used once it leaves the research setting – what incentives it creates for clinicians and patients, and what implementation might look like in practice, including how insurers and employers could build around it.

Two of the summit’s Boardroom sessions bring that tension into sharper relief, and both look likely to produce more than conversation – early indications are that at least one will feed into a published white paper, carrying the argument beyond the room. One puts clinicians and scientists from markedly different backgrounds in the same room to compare how they assess patients, prioritize interventions and decide what does or does not belong in a longevity practice – a reminder that the field is scaling before it has fully agreed on what it is. Another sets a telehealth platform, a consumer health brand and a diagnostics company against each other, each already owning one piece of the patient relationship – testing, prescribing, ongoing care – and each wanting the rest; the session asks whether the more defensible strategy is to compete for that ownership outright or interoperate and split the value, with investors effectively forcing the answer by rewarding whichever model actually returns capital.

NGL’s stated measure of success is what attendees do afterwards. Its organizers want participants to leave with an actionable blueprint, prototype or partnership rather than accumulated notes; follow-up is intended to continue beyond Osaka, including support around individual clinical or business goals.

NGL’s stated measure of success is what attendees do afterwards. In the run-up to Osaka, organizers are collecting each participant’s business goals and the connections they’re hoping to make; after the conference, that will become a personal action blueprint – agreed introductions, useful materials and follow-through on whatever was promised in the room, whether that’s a partnership lead, a research brief or something else specific to the individual. An outcomes desk will then track progress over the following year, making sure those commitments are actually kept rather than left to fade once the flight home lands.

Not gonna lie, it is an ambitious test for a conference – but a useful one. Longevity medicine has become adept at describing possible futures; the more consequential work now lies in deciding which of them can withstand evidence, implementation and the untidy business of becoming ordinary medicine.

bodyOriginal.text: Friedrich Kunath describes that he aims to make his paintings “feel like songs.” The logo for the band Oasis turns up in a top corner of “Sometimes I’m Almost There,” and there is a kind of surreal, set-like quality to his vibrant, cinematic works. “Kunath explores themes of distance and (re)location, where a longing emerges between the place you’re in and the place you’re destined to be,” says a statement for his exhibition The Nearest Faraway Place, presented by Pace in Seoul.

The artist taps into art history with compositions redolent of the tradition of Weltlandschaft , or “the world landscape,” which can be traced to the Northern Renaissance. There’s also a strong nod to the Hudson River School , which drew on 19th-century European Romanticism. Kunath tips in references to pop culture, from the ubiquitous “The End” marking the finale of theatrical releases and phrases superimposed on uncanny situations, like the eponymous painting “The most beautiful world in the world” depicting an existential aerial advertisement.

bodyOriginal.text: “Sometimes I’m Almost There” (2026), oil on canvas, 121.9 x 97.8 centimeters

Kunath is known for traversing realms of pop culture, irony, and fiction, often with a kind of nostalgic wistfulness and a tinge of the comedic. We’re initially drawn in to what appears like a traditional landscape, then quickly diverted by sticker-like additions of cartoonish, sometimes absurd characters.

As the basis of the artist’s works, romantic landscapes are already inherently invented; they may resemble real places, but the glistening light and idyllic absence of structures or people portray a kind of ideal. Kunath opens that door further. “By bringing together aesthetic contexts and familiar tropes, he materializes his subconscious,” the gallery says. “Feelings arise before we know where they come from.”

bodyOriginal.text: A new functional brain-age clock is attempting to measure how well the brain is aging and whether interventions can change its trajectory.
What if your brain could have its own biological age and, more importantly, what if that number could change?

That is the question behind Brain Years, a functional brain-age model developed through a collaboration between neurotechnology company Sens.ai and the Buck Institute for Research on Aging . Rather than looking only at the brain’s structure, the approach asks a more practical question: how well is the brain actually functioning? It is an important distinction. An MRI can show what the brain looks like. A functional assessment tries to understand what it can do.

For Dr Eric Verdin, president and CEO of the Buck Institute, that distinction is central to the wider problem of measuring aging. Traditional medicine tends to tell us whether a measurement falls inside a normal range. Aging science is increasingly interested in something more dynamic: where a person is heading.

“If you’re in the normal range, you know, there’s no taking into account of the trajectory and how close you are to becoming abnormal,” Verdin explains on the latest episode of Longevity.Technology UNLOCKED . That idea of trajectory sits at the heart of Brain Years.

Sens.ai CEO Paola Telfer and her team spent years collecting EEG and performance data from users in real-world settings, rather than relying solely on tightly controlled laboratory conditions. That created a different kind of challenge. Before AI could make sense of the data, the company needed to make sure the data itself was worth trusting.
“We knew that it’s garbage in, garbage out with AI,” Telfer says.

The company developed its own sensors and refined the system to detect when the signal might be compromised; for example, if someone is moving, chewing gum, talking or blinking excessively. The resulting dataset spans people from their early teens to their late 80s. But the real work began after the data had been collected.

The Brain Years model examines hundreds of variables derived from EEG, event-related potentials and performance during standardized tasks. Rather than deciding in advance that one particular brain signal must be the answer, the researchers used machine learning to determine which combinations were most strongly associated with chronological age and functional capacity. The result is a score intended to describe functional brain age relative to chronological age. Think of it less like an odometer and more like a weather forecast. Your chronological age tells you how long you have been alive; a brain-age clock attempts to provide another view of where your brain currently sits and potentially where it is going.

This is where the story becomes more interesting. A clock that merely tells you that your brain is older or younger than expected could be useful, but it would remain largely descriptive. The bigger promise is whether the measurement can track changes following an intervention.

Early data from Sens.ai and the Buck Institute suggests there may be something worth investigating. Telfer says an intervention study showed “5.18 years of reversal on the Brain Years measure after a two-month intervention.” But Verdin is careful about what that means.

“You’ll never hear me claiming that we’ve reverted aging,” he says. The next step, he argues, is a properly designed prospective, placebo-controlled trial that can establish whether the change represents a genuine alteration in brain aging rather than simply an improvement in test performance. That caution matters. An aging clock is ultimately a model built from measurements. If the number changes, the crucial question is whether biology changed with it.

The researchers also want to compare Brain Years with other approaches, including MRI-based clocks and blood-based proteomic measures. In other words, the future may not belong to one definitive aging clock, but to several imperfect windows that collectively give us a clearer picture.
From dementia prevention to everyday brain health

There is also something quietly radical about starting the conversation before dementia. Brain aging is often discussed as though it begins when cognitive decline becomes clinically obvious. Telfer argues for a much earlier intervention point, encompassing issues such as attention, anxiety and burnout. And that opens up a different vision of longevity medicine: not waiting for the brain to fail before measuring it, but tracking function while there is still plenty of room to intervene.

Sens.ai’s commercial path is increasingly focused on clinics, where Telfer sees the technology as a more portable and repeatable complement to expensive imaging and specialist interpretation. Verdin, meanwhile, places it within what he calls “Scientific wellness” – consumer-facing interventions subjected to the kind of scientific rigor usually associated with medicine.
That middle ground could prove important. Longevity has never suffered from a shortage of things people can buy. What it has lacked is reliable ways to determine whether those things work.

The promise of a functional brain clock, then, is not really the number itself. It is the possibility of turning brain health from something we periodically worry about into something we can measure, follow and potentially improve, while there is still time to do something about it.

articles.titleOriginal: We Are Pi's ads for Interrail break free from travel cliches to show how passengers really feel
articles.summaryOriginal: This clever poster turns a sentence into a train journey: a simple but effective design trick, delivered in style. Let's be honest, we all know what a travel ad looks like. Beautiful scenery, with not...

bodyOriginal.text: This clever poster turns a sentence into a train journey: a simple but effective design trick, delivered in style.

Let's be honest, we all know what a travel ad looks like. Beautiful scenery, with not a bulldozer or screaming infant in sight? Check. Catchy yet ultimately bland and empty slogan? Check? Smiling, impossibly attractive people? Check.

Of course, there's nothing wrong with that. Holidays for most of us are just a welcome break from everyday life, and a little bit of fantasy never did anyone any harm. And I've got nothing personally against impossibly attractive people; some of my best friends count among their number.

But if you're trying to sell consumers on something they wouldn't normally do, and in fact might be nervous of doing in a foreign country where they don't speak the lingo, you'll need to work a little harder.

That's exactly the challenge that the global brand consultancy We Are Pi , working with social agency Butterfly Effect , were presented with. They were approached by Interrail B.V, the Dutch company behind the European rail travel scheme that makes it cheap and easy to travel across the continent with a special pass.

As well as boosting the scheme, there was also a bit of brand housekeeping to do. Up until this point, Interrail B.V. had two brands for essentially the same rail pass: Interrail for people living in Europe, Eurail for visitors from elsewhere. The latter needed to be folded into the Interrail brand, following the business changing its name from Eurail B.V. to Interrail B.V. earlier in the year.

Better than flying The campaign indirectly challenges the notion that because flying is quicker, it's better. Instead, it leans into the idea that the longer journey isn't an inconvenience; it's part of the adventure, via a brand concept they've dubbed The Interrail Effect.

This was backed up by a customer survey in which around 70% of Interrail customers said their trip changed how they see the world. A similar number considered the experiences more impactful than other types of travel, and around a quarter considered it much more impactful than other holidays they'd taken.

bodyOriginal.alt: Yellow train route with text labels forming the phrase "Realising the best bit is between here and there and there" overlaid on a map of Europe for Interrail campaign

bodyOriginal.text: To get this across visually, the launch poster shows a stylised map of Europe. Running across it is a single yellow line representing a train route; only the stops aren't cities – they're words. Joining them together gives you the sentence: "Realising the best bit is between here and there."
It's a common design trick, but it works because it forces the reader to make a bit of an effort. Had the sentence been instantly legible, it wouldn't make half as much impact.

There's a nice extra touch too: the journey doesn't end with the last word; the line continues, albeit it's now dotted and straight. It's a subtle way to evoke the idea of exploring and making it up as you go along, without beating people over the head with the idea.

Creator-led campaign Another element of the campaign is a series of short video clips made by 30 creators from the US, Canada, Australia and Europe, who were asked to travel across the continent with Interrail over summer and share their experiences.

These clips sit in a comfortable space between standard YouTube shorts and glossy, cinematic films. The former would have been a bit "So what?", the second would have seemed a bit overblown for a target audience that's likely to be sleeping in the cheapest hostel. The sweet spot they've reached feels, in the words of Goldilocks, just right.
Ultimately, there's nothing particularly new in this campaign, but at the same time, there didn't need to be.

As Özlem Birkalan, chief brand and commercial officer at Interrail, puts it: "'The Interrail Effect' isn't something we invented. It's something travellers have described to us for decades, in their own words, after every journey. What's changing is that we're finally building the brand around it. Not around where people travel, but around what travelling like this does to them."

The campaign launched globally on 10 September in the UK, Australia and the US, and will roll out across a mix of paid, owned and earned channels including paid media, organic social, EDM, partnerships and PR as well as participating creators' own Instagram, TikTok and other social platforms.

bodyOriginal.text: Led by Samar Maakaroun, these two identities for a maker space and event space highlight how strong brand architecture is built on discipline, not decoration.

Msheireb Downtown Doha is a planned city in Doha, the capital of Qatar, that's designed to regenerate the historical district of Mushayrib (literally, 'a place to drink water' in Arabic). It's been promoted as being the world's first sustainable downtown regeneration project, and one of the smartest cities on Earth. And Doha Design District (DDD) is its hub for design, innovation, and collaboration.

Director Dana Kazic approached Samar Maakaroun and her team at Pentagram with a challenge: introduce two distinct spaces within the district, while strengthening, rather than fragmenting, the parent brand.

One would be a maker's space dedicated to experimentation and artistic development; the other, an event space that becomes a destination for exhibitions, events, and public engagement. They'd be positioned physically opposite each other.

Striving for connection It sounds like either a massive challenge or the stuff of nightmares, depending on how much experience you've had dealing with having to juggle the competing demands of brands and sub-brands, not to mention different languages.

In these scenarios, the client typically wants the two sub-brand spaces to feel connected. But in practice, they often get two names that share a typeface and a colour palette, but not much else. The connection is clearly expressed in a brand guideline PDF, yet never really translates to what the public actually sees and feels.

Black carrier bag with orange handles and Sada branding, displayed on a white surface in studio lighting
Mada storefront with turquoise signage and logo on white and black facade, with a blurred figure walking past

bodyOriginal.text: To avoid that scenario, Samar—whose identity for The Mosaic Rooms in London we covered back in April—and her team took the time to get things right. As they put it: "The relationship had to allow equity to move in all directions: from DDD to the sub-brands, between the sub-brands themselves, between languages, and back again into the wider district."

Naming and letter design Next up came the naming process. The team explored a range of ideas, from letter repetitions connected to the DDD symbol to Arabic words that had a spatial dimension and were easy to say out loud. The main thing was that the names needed to work together naturally and feel like two halves of a whole.

They found the solution in a pair of Arabic words that already had a relationship with each other. Mada, meaning range, reach or possibility, was chosen for the maker's space. Sada, meaning echo, was chosen for the space where finished work meets an audience.

bodyOriginal.alt: Four illuminated turquoise and black signage panels for Doha Design District displaying the mada maker space and event space branding on a white wall

bodyOriginal.text: From a visual point of view, "sada" and "mada" are built from almost identical letterforms, mirrored and rearranged, rather than drawn from scratch as two separate typefaces. Or to put it another way, one looks like the echo of another. This means the relationship between the two spaces doesn't need to be hammered home: it's immediately, instinctively obvious.

At a deeper level, there's a sense of culture and history baked into their DNA. Both names carry the letter D, which has been lifted from the existing Doha Design District symbol, while the other letterforms are inspired by the architecture of Msheireb, the downtown Doha district the whole scheme sits within.

Again, this works elegantly in making the whole brand architecture work harmoniously together. Every curve and notch in the wordmarks echoes something structural in the area, making them feel like a natural part of their surroundings, rather than something tagged on.

Key takeaway Here's what I think anyone working on a sub-brand can learn from this. It's terribly easy, especially when you're on a tight deadline, to go with the obvious solutions to making multiple brands work together. Use the same typeface, the same colour, the same grid system. And bosh! You have a unified system. Well, kinda.

bodyOriginal.alt: Neon green pixelated text and geometric shapes displayed on a black screen with cyan border, installed in a minimalist corridor with warm-lit alcoves on either side

bodyOriginal.text: This approach might look good in a presentation, but in the real world, where your designs are having to live, breathe and do their work, they run the risk of looking like an afterthought, stapled on to the parent brand rather than being an organic part of it.

What Pentagram did here was different. Rather than seeing the existing brand at surface level—the type, the colours—they delved deep into its ethos instead, and located the connective tissue that would make the new sub-brands feel naturally part of it.
The result? No one has to stand there explaining that Sada and Mada are part of the Doha Design District. It's just obvious. And that's the job.

articles.titleOriginal: Lung Fibrosis Drug Lowers Biological Age Estimates
articles.summaryOriginal: Six different aging clocks detected younger blood protein profiles in patients taking the experimental lung-fibrosis drug rentosertib. This suggests possible anti-aging effects, but separating those from the narrower benefits of treating fibrosis […]

bodyOriginal.text: Six different aging clocks detected younger blood protein profiles in patients taking the experimental lung-fibrosis drug rentosertib. This suggests possible anti-aging effects, but separating those from the narrower benefits of treating fibrosis remains a challenge [1].

The AI-developed drug Many drugs developed for particular diseases act on aging-related biological processes. That creates an opportunity: a clinical trial could investigate both whether a drug treats its intended disease and whether it has broader effects on aging. Ordinary clinical measurements cannot establish those broader effects, but we now have biological age clocks that closely track chronological age or predict mortality risk [2]. These clocks have been used in numerous trials as proxies to estimate the intervention’s effect on aging.

In a new study published in Nature Biotechnology , the researchers analyzed blood samples from a Phase 2a trial whose results were published last year [3]. That 12-week, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial tested rentosertib, an inhibitor of the kinase TNIK, which has been implicated in several aging-related processes [4].

Rentosertib was developed by the longevity biotech company Insilico, using a proprietary AI-based drug discovery platform, to treat idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF), a progressive disease in which excessive scar tissue compromises lung function. IPF is age-related, with a mean age of onset around 65 years, and aging processes such as cellular senescence and inflammation are heavily involved.
The new analysis included 42 of the trial’s 71 participants. Alongside placebo, the trial tested three regimens: 30 milligrams once daily, 30 milligrams twice daily, and 60 milligrams once daily.

Lower biological age readings The researchers used six different proteomic clocks, which analyze protein levels in blood. The proteomic clocks’ appeal is partly interpretability: researchers can identify which proteins affect the readings and connect them to known biological processes more directly than is often possible with methylation-based clocks. The clocks were developed by different teams, using data from UK Biobank, including one clock developed by Insilico itself. Four of the clocks were trained on chronological age, and two on mortality.

All six clocks detected lower predicted biological ages in patients taking rentosertib, although not at every dose or visit. After four weeks, the four chronological age-based clocks rated patients taking 60 milligrams once daily (the single-dose regimen) roughly three years younger, on average, than at the start of treatment. These changes were statistically significant compared with placebo. However, the two clocks trained to predict mortality risk did not show a significant change at that dose at week four.

Patients taking 30 milligrams twice daily (the split-dose regimen) showed the most consistent decreases across both types of clocks. The largest reductions in predicted biological age appeared by week four, with little additional change over the remaining eight weeks.

These results essentially mean that patients’ blood protein profiles became more similar to those associated with younger people. They do not, however, establish that the treated patients regained years of youth or would live longer.

Is there a broad anti-aging effect? Looking beyond the clock readings, the researchers found that treatment changed the levels of 326 blood proteins, including proteins involved in fibrosis, metabolism, and cellular stress responses. Most changes in the two higher-dose groups persisted throughout the trial or appeared later in treatment, suggesting that the drug continued affecting patients’ biology even after predicted ages plateaued.

The researchers then examined which proteins contributed most to the younger age estimates. A fibrosis-associated protein, LTBP2, stood out as a major contributor. It was used by all six clocks, which raises the question of whether their agreement mainly reflects the drug’s effect on fibrosis, rather than broader slowing of aging.

To explore whether the lower age estimates reflected more than improvement in fibrosis, the researchers compared changes in predicted age with changes in lung function. The two did not closely track each other. This suggests that improved lung function alone might not explain the clock changes, although lung function does not capture every aspect of IPF.

The team then compared the treatment-induced protein changes with differences between younger and older participants in UK Biobank. With the split dose, proteins associated with aging tended to move in the opposite direction: those found at higher levels in older people tended to decrease, and vice versa. This pattern was not statistically significant with the single daily dose.

Finally, the researchers examined proteins associated with cellular senescence. These proteins tended to increase in the placebo group but decrease with treatment, suggesting that rentosertib might reduce senescence-associated activity, although the researchers did not directly measure senescent cells in tissues.

These findings strengthen the case for investigating rentosertib as a potential geroprotector. However, because fibrosis, metabolism, and senescence are closely connected, they still cannot definitively establish whether the drug affects aging beyond its benefits for IPF.

“This study illustrates how biomarkers of aging can be incorporated into conventional clinical trials,” Vadim Gladyshev, a professor of medicine at Harvard Medical School and a coauthor of the study, told Lifespan News. “If validated more broadly, such approaches could allow us to learn not only whether a treatment affects a particular disease, but also whether it influences some aspects of aging biology.”

bodyOriginal.text: Fresh from Spain’s spectacular victory in the 2026 FIFA World Cup, Madrid is preparing for another kind of world-class gathering: one focused not on winning more years of sporting glory, but on winning more healthy years of life.

On September 30 and October 1, 2026, the International Longevity Summit Madrid 2026 will bring together leading scientists, physicians, entrepreneurs, investors and futurists to explore one of humanity’s greatest challenges—and potentially greatest opportunities: extending healthy human life.

Organized by the International Longevity Alliance, the Summit comes to a city uniquely positioned to lead the global conversation on longevity. Spain has the highest life expectancy in the European Union, while the Comunidad de Madrid has recorded the highest life expectancy of any EU region, reaching the remarkable landmark of 85.7 years according to Eurostat. Madrid may therefore be more than simply a great European capital; it could increasingly be considered a “Blue Zone 2.0”: a modern, dynamic metropolis where exceptional longevity meets cutting-edge science, biotechnology and innovation.

bodyOriginal.alt: LSM 2

bodyOriginal.text: And now, after Spain’s national team, La Roja, captured the 2026 FIFA World Cup, Spain can proudly claim another world-leading achievement. In July, Spain defeated Argentina 1–0 after extra time to win its second men’s World Cup title, adding a new chapter to a country already renowned for its health, lifestyle and longevity.

From world champions on the football field to potential champions of healthy longevity, Spain is demonstrating that the future may belong to those who know how to live—and perhaps someday live much longer.

This year, the Summit will be held at the magnificent Real Academia Nacional de Medicina de España (RANME), the Royal National Academy of Medicine of Spain, the country’s most prestigious medical institution. Founded in 1734, the Academy occupies a unique place in Spanish scientific history. The Academy is under the High Patronage of His Majesty King Felipe VI, underlining the exceptional institutional importance of the venue. The Academy is also historically associated with some of the greatest names in medicine, including Spain’s Nobel laureates Santiago Ramón y Cajal and Severo Ochoa.

Located in the historic heart of Madrid, between the Royal Palace and the Teatro Real, the RANME will provide an extraordinary setting for a conversation that could reshape the future of medicine itself.

From George Church and Ray Kurzweil to Eric Topol and Peter Diamandis The International Longevity Summit has rapidly become a meeting point for some of the world’s most influential thinkers in longevity, biotechnology, medicine and the future of humanity.

Previous editions of the International Longevity Summit in Madrid have featured an exceptional roster of speakers, including George Church , pioneering geneticist; Ray Kurzweil , futurist and inventor; Steve Horvath , creator of the epigenetic clock; Andrea Maier , longevity physician and researcher; Mehmood Khan , global health and life sciences leader; Liz Parrish , biotechnology entrepreneur; Aubrey de Grey , biomedical gerontologist; Bryan Johnson , entrepreneur and longevity pioneer; María Blasco , molecular biologist and telomere researcher; João Pedro de Magalhães , biogerontologist and aging researcher; and Michael Ringel , biotechnology and pharmaceutical executive—along with many other leading scientists, physicians, entrepreneurs, and innovators from around the world.

The program will span the biology of aging, rejuvenation biotechnology, preventive and regenerative medicine, artificial intelligence, health data, biomarkers, the longevity economy and the profound social consequences of potentially dramatic increases in human healthspan.

articles.summaryOriginal: Researchers have discovered and explained how calcium mishandling in muscle cells leads to long-term muscle weakness in older people. Calcium is not just for bones Skeletal muscle […]

bodyOriginal.text: Researchers have discovered and explained how calcium mishandling in muscle cells leads to long-term muscle weakness in older people .

Calcium is not just for bones Skeletal muscle cells use calcium ions to control how and when they contract. This activity is modulated by CaMKII, a protein kinase that also regulates muscle adaptations in response to exercise [1] and serves a great many unrelated functions throughout multiple other tissues.

In young tissues, this system works well, with exercise producing reactive oxygen species (ROS) that are used to stimulate muscle growth [1]. However, with aging, this falls apart in multiple ways: calcium ions leak out of where they are supposed to be [2], mitochondria and calcium become uncoupled [3], and, as has been well-known for decades, ROS and oxidative damage are no longer properly mitigated [4]. The authors hypothesized that CaMKII signaling is involved in this dysregulation.

Constant expression weakens muscles In their first experiment, the researchers examined the muscles of 3.7-month-old mice and compared them to those of 33-month-old mice; 33 months is exceptionally old for a mouse, and mice of that age were provided by the gerontologist Dr. Rafael deCabo. These elderly mice had significantly smaller muscles than the younger group, substantially more CaMKII in muscle tissue, and more evidence of CaMKII activity while at rest. However, the researchers noted that the biomarker they used to detect activity, pT287-CaMKII, is not entirely consistent in various muscle tissues and CaMKII can be modified in many other ways [5].

To determine the effects of constant CAMKII activity in muscle, this team developed a adeno-associated virus (AAV) that caused it to become active only in that tissue. This AAV had local effects, meaning that the researchers were able to inject it onto only one tibialis anterior muscle of each individual mouse; the identical muscle on the other side was injected with a simple fluorescent reporter protein with no significant effects. Interestingly, feedback mechanisms caused natural CAMKII to be suppressed in the muscles that were given this artificial CAMKII increase.

Within less than two months, this increase in constant CaMKII caused the targeted muscles to shrink and become pound-for-pound weaker than the unmodified muscles in the same mice; direct stimulation at multiple frequencies found that the targeted muscles were unable to exert nearly as much force. While it did not impact total mitochondrial number, it had significant negative effects on mitochondrial organization. A similar experiment with a different cohort of mice found that, after nine months, the loss of muscle mass became even more significant.

Some of this muscle loss was found to be driven by inflammation. Blocking the inflammatory signal NF-κB while activating CaMKII blunted some of the effects; the muscles in this group did not become pound-for-pound weaker, but they still lost mass.

Age-related gene expression changes Gene expression was also significantly impacted. While there were some differences, the impact of constant CaMKII expression was broadly similar to that of natural aging in muscle, and the researchers identified many biochemical pathways that are increased both by natural aging and by increased CaMKII. Most notably, iron-handling pathways were significantly disrupted by CaMKII.

The researchers also injected naturally aged mice with CN19o, which inhibits CaMKII; while individual genes were not significantly affected, the sum total of gene expression was found to move towards a more youthful phenotype. While it did not increase muscle size in 21-month-old mice, suppressing CaMKII in these mice increased their ability to contract.

The researchers hold that age-related constant CaMKII signaling is a significant contributor to sarcopenia. In youth, this signaling is beneficial, but in an aged environment, it is apparently doing more harm than good. However, the researchers did not experimentally validate why constant CaMKII activation has the mitochondrial effects it does, nor did they fully elucidate the connection between calcium and iron signaling. Further work will need to be done to determine if CaMKII is a useful target in people.
